entries.meaning: Places the main event later on the line than whatever follows after. It is the most general sequencing word in English and carries no meaning of its own beyond order — no cause, no consequence, no judgment about the size of the gap.
examples: The pharmacy closes after nine.
Call me any time after Tuesday.
After the surgery, she needed six weeks off.
He apologized only after being asked twice.
Day after day, the same gray sky.
One delay after another pushed the launch to March.
It was a quarter after three when the power came back.
The shuttle leaves at ten after the hour, every hour.
The dog took off after a squirrel and didn't come back for an hour.
Reporters have been after him for a comment all week.
She was named after her grandmother.
It's a courtyard after the Spanish style.

senses.head: Later than a point in time
body: The pharmacy closes after nine.

senses.head: Later than an event
body: After the surgery, she needed six weeks off.

senses.head: Repeated succession, in the frame [noun] after [same noun]
body: day after day

senses.head: Clock time: minutes past the hour (American)
body: a quarter after three

senses.head: In pursuit of, or in search of
body: The dog took off after a squirrel.

senses.head: In imitation of, or in honor of
body: She was named after her grandmother.

Senses 5 and 6 are not temporal at all, but they belong to the same word and appear constantly. Sense 6 is the American idiom; British English also says named for, which Americans use too but hear as slightly formal.
examples: The pharmacy closes after nine.
Call me any time after Tuesday.
After the surgery, she needed six weeks off.
He apologized only after being asked twice.
Day after day, the same gray sky.
One delay after another pushed the launch to March.
It was a quarter after three when the power came back.
The shuttle leaves at ten after the hour, every hour.
The dog took off after a squirrel and didn't come back for an hour.
Reporters have been after him for a comment all week.
She was named after her grandmother.
It's a courtyard after the Spanish style.

entries.pronunciation note: no true weak form — the vowel keeps its quality even when unstressed, which makes after one of the few prepositions a learner can always hear
entries.русский: после — позже точки или события; амер. о минутах после часа: ten after six
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or gerund (after eating) — never a finite clause. After the show ended is the conjunction, a different word class doing a different job. It does take the relative pronoun in after which (the vote, after which he resigned). After is also an adverb (we ate soon after) and an attributive adjective (the after party); the preposition always has an object.
entries.pattern: after [noun phrase] · after [verb-ing] · [measure phrase] after [noun phrase] · just, right, soon, shortly, or long after [noun phrase] · [clause], after which [clause]
entries.contrast: After is the plain word; following is its newsroom dress, subsequent to its legal one, post its finance-desk one, and none of the three is clearer. Against since: after names one later point, while since opens a stretch that runs up to now — after 2019 is any time later, since 2019 is the whole span. On the clock, after is the standard American word for minutes past the hour (ten after six) where British English says only ten past six.
entries.see also: before, since, following, post, ago, past, after (conjunction)

entries.meaning: Earlier than — with the suggestion that the earlier thing also comes first in rank or in reasoning. An American meets it in property and evidence law, in philosophy, and in nineteenth-century treatises. In a memo or an email it is dead weight, and before is the word.
examples: The easement was recorded antecedent to the sale and survived it.
Antecedent to the hearing, both sides exchanged exhibit lists.
Every effect must have a cause antecedent to it.
The duty of care is antecedent to any contract between them.
A lien antecedent to the judgment takes priority over it.
Antecedent to 1868, the state imposed no such requirement.
Nothing in the record shows an agreement antecedent to the closing.

senses.head: Earlier in time than a stated event, in formal or legal prose
body: The easement was recorded antecedent to the sale.

senses.head: Earlier in a chain of cause or reasoning, and not merely on the clock
body: Every effect has a cause antecedent to it.

senses.head: Ranking ahead of a later claim, in the law of liens and priorities
body: A mortgage antecedent to the judgment takes first position.

Sense 2 is the only one that earns five syllables, because before cannot carry the idea of logical priority — the duty is before the contract says something else. Sense 1 is before in a frock coat, and every American editor cuts it.
examples: The easement was recorded antecedent to the sale and survived it.
Antecedent to the hearing, both sides exchanged exhibit lists.
Every effect must have a cause antecedent to it.
The duty of care is antecedent to any contract between them.
A lien antecedent to the judgment takes priority over it.
Antecedent to 1868, the state imposed no such requirement.
Nothing in the record shows an agreement antecedent to the closing.

entries.pronunciation note: to reduces to /tə/ and the whole phrase flattens under the sentence stress — an-tuh-SEE-duhnt tuh
entries.русский: до, прежде — юр./книжн.: предшествующий по времени, причине или очерёдности прав
entries.register: formal — legal, philosophical, and older academic prose; dated everywhere else
entries.complement: a noun phrase (antecedent to the sale) or, far more rarely, a gerund (antecedent to filing) — never a finite clause. There is no antecedent to he filed; for a clause, use before. The gerund is grammatical on the model of prior to filing, but it is thin in real American usage and a noun phrase is the safe choice. The bare adjective (the antecedent agreement) and the grammarian's noun (the antecedent of the pronoun) are separate jobs for the same word; the preposition always has an object after to.
entries.pattern: antecedent to [noun phrase] · [noun] antecedent to [noun phrase] · logically antecedent to [noun phrase] · Antecedent to [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: Three phrases in this file mean before in a suit — prior to, previous to, and antecedent to — and this is the heaviest of the three and the only one with an extra idea in it. Antecedent to leans toward priority in a chain, not merely earlier on a clock, which is why a cause is antecedent to its effect and a recorded lien is antecedent to a later judgment. Its mirror is subsequent to. Do not confuse the preposition with the grammar term antecedent (the noun a pronoun points back to), and do not reach for it where before will do: in modern American prose it reads as period costume.
entries.see also: prior to, previous to, preparatory to, before, subsequent to, ere

entries.meaning: Places the main event earlier on the line than whatever follows before — the exact mirror of after.
examples: The mail usually comes before noon.
Get here before eight or you'll miss the opening.
Read the whole contract before signing anything.
Before the storm, nobody had bothered to trim the trees.
She quit two weeks before the merger was announced.
In the alphabet, B comes before C.
Your name comes before mine on the list.
Before long, the whole office knew.
He appeared before the zoning board three times.
The bill goes before the full Senate on Thursday.
At nineteen, she had the whole thing before her.

senses.head: Earlier than a point in time
body: We should be there before noon.

senses.head: Earlier than an event
body: Sign the lease before the walk-through.

senses.head: Earlier in an ordering or a queue, where the sequence is not literally temporal
body: B comes before C.

senses.head: In the presence of a person or body with authority to judge
body: She testified before the committee.

senses.head: Facing, or still ahead of, someone
body: The whole summer lay before them.

Sense 4 is formal and mostly spatial — you appear before a judge, a court, a board, or a congregation — but it inherits the ordering logic of senses 1 through 3: the person judged comes first in line. Sense 5 is literary and always has a stretch of time or an opportunity as its subject.
examples: The mail usually comes before noon.
Get here before eight or you'll miss the opening.
Read the whole contract before signing anything.
Before the storm, nobody had bothered to trim the trees.
She quit two weeks before the merger was announced.
In the alphabet, B comes before C.
Your name comes before mine on the list.
Before long, the whole office knew.
He appeared before the zoning board three times.
The bill goes before the full Senate on Thursday.
At nineteen, she had the whole thing before her.

entries.pronunciation note: weak /bəˈfɔr/ · buh-FOR
entries.русский: до, перед — раньше точки или события; также «перед» инстанцией (testify before)
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or gerund (before leaving) — never a finite clause. Before you leave is the conjunction. Before is also an adverb with no object at all (I've seen this movie before), which is the surest test of the difference.
entries.pattern: before [noun phrase] · before [verb-ing] · [measure phrase] before [noun phrase] · just, shortly, or long before [noun phrase] · before long
entries.contrast: Before vs. by: before Friday excludes Friday, by Friday includes it — a deadline written with before is a day tighter than most writers intend. Before vs. ago: ago counts backward from now and takes the simple past (three days ago), before counts backward from a point already in the past and goes with the past perfect (he had left three days before). Before vs. prior to: identical in meaning, and before is a syllable shorter. Before vs. until: finish it before Friday is a deadline, wait until Friday is a duration.
entries.see also: after, prior to, ahead of, ere, until, by, before (conjunction)

entries.meaning: Earlier than. You will meet it in hymns, in the King James Bible, in Shakespeare, in nineteenth-century verse, and in modern writing that is reaching for one of those. It survives in living American speech only in the fixed phrase ere long, and even that is bookish.
examples: They were on the road ere dawn.
He swore he would return ere nightfall.
Ere long, the whole village had heard.
Not a word was spoken ere the reading of the will.
Ere the year's end, three of them were dead.
Ere the last bell, the church was already full.
Ere the frost came, the last of the hay was in.

senses.head: Earlier than a point in time
body: They were on the road ere dawn.

senses.head: Earlier than an event
body: Not a word was spoken ere the reading of the will.

senses.head: In the fixed adverbial ere long, before much time has passed
body: Ere long, the whole village had heard.
Sense 3 is the only one a modern American is likely to write on purpose, and even it is a costume. Senses 1 and 2 are read, not written.
examples: They were on the road ere dawn.
He swore he would return ere nightfall.
Ere long, the whole village had heard.
Not a word was spoken ere the reading of the will.
Ere the year's end, three of them were dead.
Ere the last bell, the church was already full.
Ere the frost came, the last of the hay was in.

entries.pronunciation note: no weak form — the word is short, stressed, and identical in sound to air
entries.русский: устар./поэт. прежде, до — книжная замена before
entries.complement: noun phrase — and, in older texts, a finite clause, where it is a conjunction instead (ere the sun set). A gerund is vanishingly rare and reads as pastiche; the period pattern is a bare noun phrase. No modern American writes any of it except for deliberate period effect.
entries.pattern: ere [noun phrase] · ere long · ere [the] [time noun]
entries.contrast: A dead-plain synonym of before, with nothing added but age. Do not confuse it with the homophone e'er (a contraction of ever), with err /ɜr/ ("to make a mistake"), or with air, which it is pronounced exactly like.
entries.see also: before, prior to, nigh, hence, ere (conjunction)

entries.meaning: After, in time, with a faint suggestion that the second event grew out of the first.
examples: Following the vote, the chairman resigned.
A press conference is scheduled following the hearing.
Three stores on Main closed following the flood.
Following two years of losses, the company sold its warehouse.
The reception begins immediately following the ceremony.
Following his release, he moved to Tucson and said nothing more about it.
Following the recall, the company replaced its entire safety team.

senses.head: Later in time than a named event
body: Following the vote, the chairman resigned.

senses.head: In the wake of, shading into cause
body: Three stores closed following the flood.

That second sense is why press releases like it: following lets a writer imply a connection without claiming one. In careful prose that is a reason to distrust the word rather than a reason to use it.
examples: Following the vote, the chairman resigned.
A press conference is scheduled following the hearing.
Three stores on Main closed following the flood.
Following two years of losses, the company sold its warehouse.
The reception begins immediately following the ceremony.
Following his release, he moved to Tucson and said nothing more about it.
Following the recall, the company replaced its entire safety team.

entries.pronunciation note: no weak form — the stress stays on the first syllable and nothing reduces, which is part of why the word feels heavy next to after
entries.русский: после, вслед за — нейтр.-книжн., газетный оборот вместо after
entries.complement: a noun phrase, characteristically one naming an event (following the announcement). A gerund is grammatical but clumsy, and a finite clause is impossible — there is no following the vote was counted. Note that the same string is also a present participle (the dog following me) and an adjective (the following week).
entries.pattern: Following [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause] following [noun phrase] · immediately following [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: After means the same thing and is never ambiguous; following can be misread as the verb, which is why Following the mayor, the reporters filed out stalls a reader for half a second. Against subsequent to, following at least sounds like English. Reserve it for cases where the noun really is an event and after has already been used twice in the paragraph.
entries.see also: after, prior to, subsequent to, post, pending, given

entries.meaning: Earlier than a coming event, and usually in preparation for it. The phrase is four syllables where before is two, so it earns its place only when the preparation is the point.
examples: Crews sandbagged the levee in advance of the storm.
Please submit your questions in advance of the meeting.
She trained for six months in advance of the race.
In advance of filing, the firm circulated a draft to the client.
Both sides filed briefs in advance of Tuesday's hearing.
The hotel needs a deposit two weeks in advance of your stay.
In advance of the audit, the department rebuilt its whole ledger.

senses.head: Early, in preparation for a coming event
body: Crews sandbagged the levee in advance of the storm.

senses.head: In the run-up to a scheduled event, without the preparation sense
body: Both sides filed briefs in advance of the hearing.
Sense 1 is the one that justifies the phrase. Sense 2 is the newsroom use, where it competes directly with ahead of and loses on length.
examples: Crews sandbagged the levee in advance of the storm.
Please submit your questions in advance of the meeting.
She trained for six months in advance of the race.
In advance of filing, the firm circulated a draft to the client.
Both sides filed briefs in advance of Tuesday's hearing.
The hotel needs a deposit two weeks in advance of your stay.
In advance of the audit, the department rebuilt its whole ledger.

entries.pronunciation note: of reduces to /əv/ or bare /ə/ — in ad-VANSS uh
entries.русский: заранее до, в преддверии — офиц.: до события, часто с подготовкой к нему
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (in advance of filing) — never a finite clause. There is no in advance of he arrived; for a clause, use before. The bare adverbial in advance (pay in advance, a week in advance) takes no object at all and is the commoner form by far.
entries.pattern: in advance of [noun phrase] · in advance of [verb-ing] · In advance of [event], [clause] · [quantity of time] in advance (adverb, no object)
entries.contrast: In advance of is not a free synonym of before. It carries the idea of preparation — you do something early so as to be ready for what is coming. She trained in advance of the race is idiomatic because the training served the race; she was born in advance of the war is not, because birth prepares for nothing. Plain before has no such restriction, which is why it fits everywhere this phrase does and many places it does not. Against ahead of: the two overlap almost completely in the run-up sense, and ahead of is shorter. Against prior to: prior to is pure sequence with no preparation in it.
entries.see also: ahead of, before, prior to, on the eve of, by

entries.meaning: In the stretch of time that follows a destructive event and is still shaped by it. The word is a farming term — math is an old word for a mowing, and the aftermath was the second growth that came up after the first cut — and that is exactly the image: what comes up in ground the event has already gone over.
examples: In the aftermath of the flood, half the block never came back.
In the aftermath of the shooting, the school stayed closed a week.
Insurance rates doubled in the aftermath of the fire.
In the immediate aftermath of the crash, nobody knew how many were aboard.
In the aftermath of the scandal, three board members resigned within a month.
In the aftermath of the war, the city rebuilt the whole downtown in brick.
The rule was written in the aftermath of a collapse nobody had planned for.

senses.head: In the period following a disaster or a shock
body: In the aftermath of the flood, half the block moved out.

senses.head: In the period following a political or institutional upheaval, with the consequences as the point
body: In the aftermath of the scandal, three directors resigned.

senses.head: In the first hours or days after a disaster, in the narrowed frame with "immediate."
body: In the immediate aftermath of the crash, nobody knew how many were aboard.
Sense 3 is the one that pins the phrase down. Without immediate the stretch floats: the aftermath of a storm is a week, the aftermath of a war can be a decade, and the phrase itself never says which.
examples: In the aftermath of the flood, half the block never came back.
In the aftermath of the shooting, the school stayed closed a week.
Insurance rates doubled in the aftermath of the fire.
In the immediate aftermath of the crash, nobody knew how many were aboard.
In the aftermath of the scandal, three board members resigned within a month.
In the aftermath of the war, the city rebuilt the whole downtown in brick.
The rule was written in the aftermath of a collapse nobody had planned for.

entries.pronunciation note: the is /ði/ before the vowel of aftermath, and of reduces to /əv/ or bare /ə/ — in thee AF-ter-math uh
entries.русский: после, в период после — о последствиях катастрофы или потрясения
entries.register: neutral to formal — journalistic and historical
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a disaster, a shock, or an upheaval — the flood, the shooting, the crash, the war. No gerund: in the aftermath of resigning is possible but stiff, and in the aftermath of his resignation is the idiomatic repair. No finite clause. The article is fixed — in aftermath of is not English — and the noun aftermath also stands alone (the aftermath was worse than the storm), where it is not a preposition at all.
entries.pattern: In the aftermath of [event], [clause] · [clause] in the aftermath of [event] · in the immediate aftermath of [event]
entries.contrast: Against in the wake of, its close twin: both mean "in the period following, and shaped by," and in the wake of is the wider of the two — a policy can follow in the wake of a report, where the aftermath of a report is odd unless the report did damage. The restriction worth memorizing is the event: an aftermath is the bad stretch after something bad. In the aftermath of the wedding is a joke; in the aftermath of the fire is not. Against after and following, which are neutral about consequence, and against on the heels of, which stresses how fast the second thing came rather than how much wreckage the first left.
entries.see also: after, following, post, on the eve of, in the wake of, on the heels of

entries.meaning: Immediately before a significant event, with the event's importance built into the phrase. The noun eve is a worn-down even, the old word for evening, which survives independently in Christmas Eve and New Year's Eve.
examples: They arrived on the eve of the wedding.
On the eve of the election, the polls finally tightened.
The company announced layoffs on the eve of the holidays.
On the eve of war, the embassy burned its files.
He resigned on the eve of the vote he was certain to lose.
On the eve of the launch, a sensor failed and cost them the window.
On the eve of the trial, the state offered a plea.

senses.head: On the day or night immediately before, literally
body: They arrived on the eve of the wedding.

senses.head: In the last stretch before a momentous event, figuratively
body: On the eve of the election, the polls tightened.
Sense 2 has no fixed length and takes all the weight. If the event is not genuinely momentous, the phrase reads as inflation and before is the honest word.
examples: They arrived on the eve of the wedding.
On the eve of the election, the polls finally tightened.
The company announced layoffs on the eve of the holidays.
On the eve of war, the embassy burned its files.
He resigned on the eve of the vote he was certain to lose.
On the eve of the launch, a sensor failed and cost them the window.
On the eve of the trial, the state offered a plea.

entries.pronunciation note: of reduces to /əv/ or bare /ə/; the is /ði/ before the vowel of eve
entries.русский: накануне — в день перед событием или в последний период перед ним
entries.register: formal to journalistic — heavily used in news writing and history
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming an event, and essentially nothing else (on the eve of the election, on the eve of war). No gerund — on the eve of signing is possible but stiff, and on the eve of the signing is the idiomatic repair. No finite clause. The article is fixed: on eve of is headline clipping, not prose.
entries.pattern: on the eve of [event noun] · On the eve of [event], [clause] · [clause] on the eve of [event]
entries.contrast: Literally it means the night or the day before, and in on the eve of Christmas it still does; figuratively it has loosened to mean "in the last stretch before," which can be a week or a year. That drift is why editors distrust it. Against ahead of and in advance of, both of which are neutral, on the eve of is the dramatic option — it exists to make the coming event sound momentous, so it wants a war, an election, a launch, or a verdict, not a dentist appointment.
entries.see also: ahead of, in advance of, before, prior to, upon

entries.meaning: After a named event or era. The usage grew out of postwar and post-Watergate, where the prefix was doing real work, and then broke free of the hyphen sometime in the late twentieth century. American editors split on it: it is unremarkable in an earnings call and conspicuous in a magazine.
examples: Margins recovered post the merger.
Post pandemic, nobody wants five days a week in the office.
Head count is down twelve percent post the reorganization.
We'll revisit the forecast post earnings.
Post the recall, the stock never fully came back.
Everything in that neighborhood went up post-war.
Post the split, the two halves were worth more than the whole had been.

senses.head: After a specific event
body: Margins recovered post the merger.

senses.head: After an era, usually with no article
body: Post pandemic, nobody wants five days in the office.
examples: Margins recovered post the merger.
Post pandemic, nobody wants five days a week in the office.
Head count is down twelve percent post the reorganization.
We'll revisit the forecast post earnings.
Post the recall, the stock never fully came back.
Everything in that neighborhood went up post-war.
Post the split, the two halves were worth more than the whole had been.

entries.pronunciation note: no weak form — the diphthong survives even unstressed, which is one reason the word still sounds like a prefix that got loose
entries.русский: после — деловой и газетный жаргон: post the merger «после слияния»
entries.register: informal-to-neutral in business, finance, tech, and journalism; still rejected by conservative editors
entries.type: simple (a preposition clipped out of the Latin prefix post-)
entries.complement: a noun phrase, nearly always one naming an event or an era (post the merger, post pandemic). No gerund, no clause, and no article is required. It is far commoner as the hyphenated prefix (postwar, post-9/11, post-op), and that is the safe form in edited prose.
entries.pattern: post [event noun] · post [era noun] · post-[noun] as an attributive modifier
entries.contrast: It is after, in one syllable, borrowed out of a prefix. Against following and subsequent to — which are at least whole English words — post still reads as in-group jargon: post the acquisition is finance-speak for after the acquisition. The mirror form pre (pre the merger) exists but is rarer and sounds more British. When in doubt, hyphenate it onto a noun and it stops being controversial.
entries.see also: after, following, subsequent to, prior to

entries.meaning: Before, and as a preparation for. Nineteenth-century business and legal prose used the phrase freely; modern American writing keeps it in military orders, procedural manuals, and formal narration, where one step is being logged as a step toward the next.
examples: He cleared his desk preparatory to leaving for good.
The crew rigged the lines preparatory to casting off.
Two divisions were moved south preparatory to the landing.
She sold the house preparatory to moving to Phoenix.
Preparatory to filing, counsel circulated a draft of the complaint.
The company took a charge preparatory to the spin-off.
He cleared his throat preparatory to saying something he had clearly rehearsed.

senses.head: Before a stated action, as a step toward it, with a gerund
body: He cleared his desk preparatory to leaving.

senses.head: Before a stated event, in preparation for it, with a noun phrase
body: Troops moved south preparatory to the landing.

Sense 1 is where the phrase does work that nothing shorter does, because in preparation for cannot take a verb. In sense 2, with a plain noun after it, in preparation for is the more natural American choice and ahead of is shorter than either.
examples: He cleared his desk preparatory to leaving for good.
The crew rigged the lines preparatory to casting off.
Two divisions were moved south preparatory to the landing.
She sold the house preparatory to moving to Phoenix.
Preparatory to filing, counsel circulated a draft of the complaint.
The company took a charge preparatory to the spin-off.
He cleared his throat preparatory to saying something he had clearly rehearsed.

entries.pronunciation note: weak /prəˈpærəˌtɔri tə/ — the first syllable reduces to /prə/ and to to /tə/ — pruh-PAIR-uh-tor-ee tuh
entries.русский: перед тем как, в порядке подготовки к — офиц./воен.: как шаг к действию
entries.register: formal — legal, military, procedural, and dated business prose
entries.complement: a noun phrase or a gerund (preparatory to filing, preparatory to moving out) — never a finite clause. There is no preparatory to he filed. The gerund is in fact the commoner complement, and that is what separates this phrase from previous to and prior to, where the noun phrase dominates. The bare adjective (preparatory work, a preparatory school) drops the to and is a different job.
entries.pattern: preparatory to [verb-ing] · preparatory to [noun phrase] · [clause] preparatory to [verb-ing] · Preparatory to [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: It is before plus a purpose: whatever comes first is done in order to get ready for what follows, which is the same restriction in advance of carries and the one prior to does not. He resigned preparatory to running for office says the resignation served the campaign; he resigned prior to running for office says only that it came first. Against in preparation for, which is plainer, commoner in American writing, and takes a noun phrase only — the gerund frame is the one place preparatory to still earns its keep. Never use it where nothing is being prepared for: she was born preparatory to the war is nonsense.
entries.see also: in advance of, ahead of, prior to, previous to, antecedent to, before, in anticipation of

entries.meaning: Earlier than. It carries nothing that before does not, and in American English it survives mainly in historical writing and in the fixed backward-pointing previous to that.
examples: Previous to 1920, women could not vote in most state elections.
Previous to the hearing, neither side had seen the report.
He had held two other pastorates previous to this one.
Previous to enlisting, he had never been out of the county.
Nothing in the file is dated previous to the closing.
She runs a print shop; previous to that, she taught school.
Previous to the fire, the building had housed a bank.

senses.head: Earlier than a stated event or date
body: Previous to 1920, women could not vote in most states.

senses.head: Earlier than a stated action, with a gerund
body: Previous to enlisting, he had never left the county.

senses.head: In the fixed backward-pointing idiom, before the time just mentioned
body: She taught in Ohio; previous to that, she had been in the Navy.

Sense 3 is the only one an American is likely to say out loud, and even it competes with the plainer before that. Note that senses 1 and 2 both pull the past perfect after them, because the sentence is already standing at one past point and looking further back.
examples: Previous to 1920, women could not vote in most state elections.
Previous to the hearing, neither side had seen the report.
He had held two other pastorates previous to this one.
Previous to enlisting, he had never been out of the county.
Nothing in the file is dated previous to the closing.
She runs a print shop; previous to that, she taught school.
Previous to the fire, the building had housed a bank.

entries.pronunciation note: to reduces to /tə/ — PREE-vee-uhs tuh
entries.русский: до, прежде — книжн. и устаревающее; то же, что before, но тяжеловеснее
entries.register: formal and dated — legal, historical, and older American prose
entries.complement: a noun phrase or a gerund (previous to signing) — never a finite clause. There is no previous to he signed; for a clause, use before. In the fixed previous to that the object is a pronoun pointing back at the last thing said. The adjective previous by itself takes no to (the previous tenant), and the adverb previously takes no object at all.
entries.pattern: previous to [noun phrase] · previous to [verb-ing] · Previous to [noun phrase], [clause] · previous to that
entries.contrast: An exact synonym of prior to, which is itself an exact synonym of before. Of the three, before is the one to write, prior to is the one American legal and medical drafting actually uses, and previous to is the one that sounds like 1890 — rare enough now that a reader notices it. Usage guides have been striking it out since Fowler. Note that the adverb previously is alive and unremarkable (he had previously worked in Boston); it is only the preposition that is dated.
entries.see also: prior to, antecedent to, preparatory to, before, subsequent to, ere

entries.meaning: Earlier than. The phrase is built on the adjective prior ("earlier, previous"), which is why it attracts writers who want a sentence to sound procedural. In ordinary prose it adds length, not precision: prior to the meeting and before the meeting are the same statement.
examples: All materials must be submitted prior to the deadline.
Prior to 2018, the building had no sprinkler system.
Patients should fast for eight hours prior to the procedure.
Prior to signing, review the indemnification clause.
He held two other posts prior to his appointment as chief.
Any defect reported prior to delivery is the seller's problem.
Prior to dispensing the medication, the pharmacist must verify the allergy list.

senses.head: Earlier than a stated event
body: All materials must be submitted prior to the deadline.

senses.head: Earlier than a date or a year, as a background marker
body: Prior to 2018, the building had no sprinkler system.

senses.head: Earlier than a stated action, with a gerund
body: Prior to signing, review the indemnification clause.
Sense 3 is the one that carries real weight in drafting, because it attaches a requirement to an act rather than to a clock: prior to signing binds whoever signs, whenever that happens.
examples: All materials must be submitted prior to the deadline.
Prior to 2018, the building had no sprinkler system.
Patients should fast for eight hours prior to the procedure.
Prior to signing, review the indemnification clause.
He held two other posts prior to his appointment as chief.
Any defect reported prior to delivery is the seller's problem.
Prior to dispensing the medication, the pharmacist must verify the allergy list.

entries.pronunciation note: to reduces to /tə/ — PRY-er tuh
entries.русский: до, ранее — офиц.-юр. канцелярский эквивалент before
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (prior to signing) — never a finite clause. For a clause you need before, since there is no prior to he arrived.
entries.pattern: prior to [noun phrase] · prior to [verb-ing] · [clause] prior to [noun phrase] · Prior to [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: It means before, exactly and only, in three syllables instead of two, and every American usage guide tells you to cut it. Keep it in contracts, protocols, and medical charts, where it is house style and where prior pairs with subsequent. Do not stretch it to mean in advance of in the sense of preparation — she trained in advance of the race is not she trained prior to the race.
entries.see also: before, ahead of, in advance of, subsequent to, post, prior to (complex)

entries.meaning: Opens a stretch of time that starts at a named point and runs up to the present moment. The "runs to now" part is built into the word, and it is why the main verb must be a perfect: the stretch is still open.
examples: We've been waiting since eight o'clock.
She's lived in Tucson since 2019.
Nothing has been the same since the fire.
He hasn't touched a piano since leaving school.
Ever since the surgery, he's walked with a cane.
By March, she had not heard from him since the funeral.
The building had stood empty since the previous tenant's bankruptcy.

senses.head: From a past point up to now
body: We've been waiting since eight.

senses.head: From a past point up to some other past point, with the past perfect
body: By March he had not written since the funeral.
examples: We've been waiting since eight o'clock.
She's lived in Tucson since 2019.
Nothing has been the same since the fire.
He hasn't touched a piano since leaving school.
Ever since the surgery, he's walked with a cane.

The building had stood empty since the previous tenant's bankruptcy.

entries.pronunciation note: weak /səns/ in fast speech
entries.русский: с (такого-то момента) — от точки в прошлом до сих пор; длительность не мерит (ср. for)
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a point in time (since Monday, since 2019, since the accident), a time adverb (since then, since yesterday), or a gerund (since leaving school). Never a length of time — since three years is the commonest single error in this file, and the word for a length is for. With a finite clause it is a conjunction (since I moved here), and with no object at all an adverb (I haven't seen her since).
entries.pattern: [perfect verb] ... since [point in time] · since [verb-ing] · ever since [point in time] · Since [point in time], [perfect clause] · since when (fixed)
entries.contrast: for / since / ago is the triangle: for takes a length (for three years), since takes a starting point (since 2022), and ago takes a length and counts backward from now (three years ago). Since also demands the perfect in the main clause — She has lived here since 2019, never she lives here since 2019. The causal since ("because") is the conjunction, not this word, and since meaning "afterward" (he has since retired) is an adverb.
entries.see also: ago, as of, until, for, from, since (conjunction)

entries.meaning: After. The adjective subsequent means "coming later," and the phrase inherits that and nothing more. It carries no implication of consequence, despite the family resemblance to consequent: subsequent to the audit says only that something happened later, not that the audit caused it.
examples: Subsequent to the audit, three controls were rewritten.
Any claim arising subsequent to the closing date is the buyer's.
Subsequent to filing, the plaintiff amended the complaint twice.
The defect was discovered subsequent to delivery.
Subsequent to his resignation, the department was reorganized.
Two findings were disclosed subsequent to the balance-sheet date.
Subsequent to receiving notice, the tenant has ten days to cure.

senses.head: After a stated event
body: Subsequent to the audit, three controls were rewritten.

senses.head: After a date or a cutoff, in claims, warranties, and financial statements
body: Any claim arising subsequent to the closing date is the buyer's.

senses.head: After a stated action, with a gerund
body: Subsequent to filing, the plaintiff amended the complaint twice.

Sense 2 is the one with a technical life of its own: accountants call anything that happens after the balance-sheet date a subsequent event, and the phrase is the standard label for it. Senses 1 and 3 are ordinary after in a suit.
examples: Subsequent to the audit, three controls were rewritten.
Any claim arising subsequent to the closing date is the buyer's.
Subsequent to filing, the plaintiff amended the complaint twice.
The defect was discovered subsequent to delivery.
Subsequent to his resignation, the department was reorganized.
Two findings were disclosed subsequent to the balance-sheet date.
Subsequent to receiving notice, the tenant has ten days to cure.

entries.pronunciation note: to reduces to /tə/ — SUB-si-kwuhnt tuh
entries.русский: после — юр./офиц. канцелярский эквивалент after
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause. There is no subsequent to he resigned; use after with a clause.
entries.pattern: subsequent to [noun phrase] · subsequent to [verb-ing] · [clause] subsequent to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The mirror of prior to, and heavier still: five syllables for a word of two. It exists mainly so that legal drafting can pair prior to with something symmetrical. Outside contracts and audit reports, write after.
entries.see also: after, following, prior to, post, subsequent to (complex)

entries.meaning: At the moment of the stated event, and therefore immediately after it. This is the one job in modern American English where upon is not merely a dressed-up on — it is the standard way contracts, invoices, and official notices attach an obligation to a triggering event.
examples: Payment is due upon receipt.
Upon arrival, please check in at the front desk.
The estate passes to her children upon her death.
Upon signing, you have three business days to cancel.
Upon hearing the verdict, he sat back down without a word.
The balance becomes payable upon completion of the work.
Once upon a time, this was all farmland.
Once upon a time there were three sawmills on this river.

senses.head: At the moment a stated event occurs
body: Payment is due upon receipt.

senses.head: With a gerund: as soon as someone does something
body: Upon signing, you have three days to cancel.

senses.head: The frozen storytelling opener
body: Once upon a time...
examples: Payment is due upon receipt.
Upon arrival, please check in at the front desk.
The estate passes to her children upon her death.
Upon signing, you have three business days to cancel.
Upon hearing the verdict, he sat back down without a word.
The balance becomes payable upon completion of the work.
Once upon a time, this was all farmland.
Once upon a time there were three sawmills on this river.

entries.pronunciation note: also /əˈpɔn/ · uh-PAWN · the first syllable is already reduced to /ə/ and never takes stress, so there is no further weak form
entries.русский: по, при — книжн.: upon receipt «по получении», upon signing «при подписании»
entries.register: formal — contracts, notices, and fixed phrases
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming an event (upon arrival, upon receipt) or a gerund (upon signing, upon hearing the verdict) — never a finite clause. The gerund is the construction that keeps the word alive in modern American writing.
entries.pattern: upon [event noun] · upon [verb-ing] · Upon [noun phrase], [clause] · on or upon [receipt, arrival, completion, delivery]
entries.contrast: In the time sense upon means "at the moment of, and immediately after," compressing a whole clause: upon arrival is as soon as he arrived in two words. Plain on does the same job and is shorter (on arrival, on receipt); the two are interchangeable here and upon is the drafting choice. Against after, which allows any interval: after signing could be a week later, upon signing is that instant. The contact and movement senses live in upon.
entries.see also: on, after, as of, effective, upon (movement)

entries.meaning: Fixes an event to a point in a life rather than to a point on the calendar. It is the standard frame of obituaries, biographies, medical histories, and legal findings, and it is one of the very few time phrases in English whose object must ordinarily be a number.
examples: She published her first novel at the age of twenty-three.
He started at the mill at the age of fifteen and stayed forty years.
My grandmother learned to drive at the age of sixty.
At the age of four, he could already read the sports page out loud.
The diagnosis usually comes at the age of seven or eight.
The trust distributes the principal at the age of majority.
She died at the age of ninety-one, in the house she was born in.

senses.head: At the point in a life named by a number
body: She published her first book at the age of twenty-three.

senses.head: At a legally or ritually defined stage, in fixed terms
body: The trust pays out at the age of majority.

The clipping is worth a note of its own. At age fifteen is not casual English — it is the form American newspapers, medical charts, and court opinions prefer, and it drops both the article and the of. What it cannot do is stand at the head of a sentence as comfortably: At the age of fifteen, he started at the mill reads better than At age fifteen, he started at the mill.
examples: She published her first novel at the age of twenty-three.
He started at the mill at the age of fifteen and stayed forty years.
My grandmother learned to drive at the age of sixty.
At the age of four, he could already read the sports page out loud.
The diagnosis usually comes at the age of seven or eight.

She died at the age of ninety-one, in the house she was born in.

entries.pronunciation note: at reduces to /ət/, the is /ði/ before the vowel of age, and of to /əv/ or bare /ə/ — uht thee AYJ uh
entries.русский: в возрасте (скольких-то лет) — указывает возраст в момент события
entries.complement: a number, and in ordinary use nothing else — at the age of six, at the age of ninety-two. A noun follows only in a closed set of fixed legal and religious terms (at the age of consent, at the age of majority, at the age of reason). No gerund, no finite clause. The article is fixed: at age of six is not English, though the clipped at age six — no article, no of — is standard American and is commoner in print than the full phrase.
entries.pattern: at the age of [number] · At the age of [number], [clause] · at age [number] (the clipped American form) · at the age of [consent, majority, reason] (fixed terms)
entries.variants: at age [number] (the standard American clipping — at age fifteen), aged [number] (chiefly British and newspaper style — a boy aged fifteen)
entries.contrast: The live choice here is length, not meaning: at the age of six, at age six, and plain at six all say the same thing. American writing uses the middle one most; the full phrase survives wherever a bare number would be misread, since at six also means six o'clock. Against by the age of, which is a deadline rather than a point — she was reading by the age of four claims four or earlier. Against from the age of, which opens a span (from the age of twelve he worked summers). And note going on, the colloquial hedge for an age not quite reached (going on eighty).
entries.see also: at the time of, by the end of, come, going on, at

entries.term: at the beginning of/at the start of
entries.ipa: /ət ðə bɪˈɡɪnɪŋ əv/, /ət ðə ˈstɑrt əv/
entries.respell: uht thuh bih-GIN-ing uhv, uht thuh START uhv
entries.meaning: Pins an event to the near edge of a period or a process. Everything the frame does is edge-work: it says the event sat at the opening of the span, not somewhere inside it.
examples: Rent is due at the beginning of the month, not the end.
At the start of the meeting, she handed out the revised numbers.
The furnace quit at the beginning of the coldest week of the year.
At the start of the season nobody picked them to finish above .500.
At the beginning of his career he covered high school football for forty dollars a game.
We heard about the change right at the start of the shift.
At the beginning of the semester the class had thirty students in it.

senses.head: At the opening of a period on the calendar
body: Rent is due at the beginning of the month.

senses.head: At the opening of an event or a process already under way
body: At the start of the meeting, she handed out the numbers.

senses.head: At the first stage of a career, a life, or a long undertaking
body: At the beginning of his career he covered high school sports.

Choosing between the two wordings is a matter of rhythm and register, not of meaning. Start is the shorter, blunter, more spoken word and dominates in sports, work, and scheduling; beginning is the one that fits a life, a book, or a century. Neither can be shortened to at the beginning when a period is named — the of is not optional.
examples: Rent is due at the beginning of the month, not the end.
At the start of the meeting, she handed out the revised numbers.
The furnace quit at the beginning of the coldest week of the year.
At the start of the season nobody picked them to finish above .500.
At the beginning of his career he covered high school football for forty dollars a game.
We heard about the change right at the start of the shift.
At the beginning of the semester the class had thirty students in it.

entries.pronunciation note: at reduces to /ət/ and of to /əv/ or bare /ə/ — uht thuh bih-GIN-ing uh, uht thuh START uh
entries.русский: в начале — в первый момент периода, события или процесса
entries.register: neutral — at the start of a shade more spoken, at the beginning of a shade more written
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a period or a process with a shape — the year, the semester, the meeting, her career. A gerund is grammatical but clumsy and rare: at the beginning of writing the report is repaired either to when he began writing the report or to at the beginning of the report. No finite clause. The article is fixed; bare at start of is form-field clipping. Note that at first, to start with, and in the beginning are adverbials with no object at all.
entries.pattern: at the beginning of [period] · at the start of [period] · At the start of [period], [clause] · right at the start of [period] · from the start of [period]
entries.variants: at the start of and at the beginning of are interchangeable in nearly every context; at the outset of is the formal third (at the outset of the trial); at the top of is the broadcast and business idiom for the near edge of an hour or a meeting (at the top of the hour, at the top of the call); at the head of is spatial, not temporal
entries.contrast: Its mirror is at the end of, and the two frames behave identically. Against near and toward, which both back off the edge: at the start of the month is the first day or two, toward the beginning of the month is looser and still moving. Against from the start of, which is the difference between a point and a span — at the start of the season names a moment, from the start of the season opens a stretch that runs on. And against the objectless at first, which cannot name the period it belongs to.
entries.see also: at the end of, at the time of, near, toward, beginning, starting, from

entries.meaning: Pins an event to the far edge of a period or a process — the exact mirror of at the beginning of.
examples: The lease is up at the end of June.
At the end of the interview they asked for three references.
We settle up at the end of every month.
At the end of the season half the roster was gone.
At the end of his life he moved back to the farm he grew up on.
Her name is in the credits at the very end of the reel.
At the end of the day, the numbers still had to work.

senses.head: At the closing moment of a period
body: The lease is up at the end of June.

senses.head: At the close of an event or a process
body: At the end of the interview, they asked for references.

senses.head: At the last stage of a life, a career, or a long run
body: At the end of his life he moved back to the farm.

senses.head: In the fixed idiom "at the end of the day": when everything is taken into account
body: At the end of the day, the numbers still have to work.

Sense 4 has no time in it at all. It is the American workplace's favorite filler, and a reader who hears it as a clock reference will misparse the sentence — which is the argument for cutting it and writing ultimately, or nothing.
examples: The lease is up at the end of June.
At the end of the interview they asked for three references.
We settle up at the end of every month.
At the end of the season half the roster was gone.
At the end of his life he moved back to the farm he grew up on.
Her name is in the credits at the very end of the reel.
At the end of the day, the numbers still had to work.

entries.pronunciation note: at reduces to /ət/, the is /ði/ before the vowel of end, and of to /əv/ or bare /ə/ — uht thee END uh
entries.русский: в конце — в последний момент периода; at the end of the day «в конечном счёте»
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a period or a process (the month, the meeting, his life). No gerund — at the end of eating is not English, and the repair is when he finished eating. No finite clause. The article is fixed. The same frame is also spatial (at the end of the hall) and idiomatic (at the end of the day), and both take a noun phrase in exactly the same way.
entries.pattern: at the end of [period] · At the end of [period], [clause] · at the very end of [period] · at the end of the day (fixed idiom)
entries.variants: at the close of (formal — at the close of business, at the close of the century), at the tail end of (informal, and always a little grudging)
entries.contrast: Against by the end of, which is the contrast to drill: at the end of the month names a moment, by the end of the month names a deadline that anything earlier also satisfies. A report due at the end of the month is wanted on the 30th; due by the end of the month, it can land on the 3rd. Against near and toward, which stop short of the edge. Against the objectless in the end, which means "finally" and names no period. And note at the end of the day, which in American English is nearly always the figurative filler meaning "when everything is considered" — a phrase about reasoning, not about five o'clock.
entries.see also: at the beginning of/at the start of, by the end of, near, toward, until, through

entries.meaning: Pins one event to the moment another event happened. It is the phrase that legal, insurance, and academic writing reach for when exact simultaneity is the thing at issue — a policy in force, an age, an address, a state of knowledge.
examples: She was twenty-six at the time of the crash.
At the time of writing, the bill still had not been signed.
At the time of the merger, the company had nine hundred employees.
The policy had lapsed at the time of the fire.
Payment is collected at the time of booking, not at check-in.
He was living in Denver at the time of his father's death.
At the time of filing, neither party had counsel.

senses.head: At the moment a stated event occurred
body: She was twenty-six at the time of the crash.

senses.head: With a gerund, at the moment of doing something
body: At the time of writing, the bill had not been signed.

senses.head: In the transactional frame, at the moment a transaction takes place
body: Payment is collected at the time of booking.
Sense 3 is the one that drops its article on forms and signs. At time of purchase is standard on a receipt and wrong in a sentence; write at the time of purchase in prose.
examples: She was twenty-six at the time of the crash.
