entries.pronunciation note: at reduces to /ət/ and of to /əv/ or bare /ə/ — uht thuh TYME uh
entries.русский: во время, на момент — в момент указанного события или действия
entries.register: neutral to formal — legal, insurance, journalistic, and academic
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming an event or a period (at the time of the accident), or a gerund (at the time of writing, at the time of filing) — never a finite clause. There is no at the time of he arrived; for a clause, use when. The frame at the time that [clause] is not an exception, since the clause there sits inside the noun phrase the time. The article is fixed in prose: bare at time of survives only as form-field clipping (at time of purchase, at time of service), which is why you meet it on receipts and nowhere else.
entries.pattern: at the time of [event noun] · at the time of [verb-ing] · At the time of [event], [clause] · at time of [purchase, service, sale] (fixed transactional clipping)
entries.contrast: Against during, which spreads an event across a whole period: an accident has no inside, so during the accident is odd where at the time of the accident pins a single moment. Against when, which is shorter but needs a subject and a tense — at the time of writing is the phrase's one indispensable use, because when I write this says something else. Against as of: as of this writing dates the claim from outside and is the commoner American business form; at the time of writing puts the writer inside the moment.
entries.see also: during, in the middle of, in the course of, as of, upon, at, on

entries.meaning: Names the stretch that falls inside two stated edges, or in the gap that separates two recurring events.
examples: The pharmacy is closed between one and two.
I'll call you sometime between Tuesday and Friday.
Between 1994 and 2001, the population doubled.
Between finishing school and starting the job, she spent a summer in Maine.
She grades papers between classes.
The house sat empty between tenants for most of that year.
He wrote three novels between teaching jobs.
There's a lot to do between now and Friday.
Two meetings ran long, and I ate lunch somewhere in between.
Between you and me, the deadline was never real.

senses.head: A window bounded by two stated times
body: The pharmacy is closed between 1 and 2.

senses.head: The interval separating two recurring events
body: She grades papers between classes.

senses.head: The stretch from now to a stated future edge, in the fixed frame between now and [time]
body: We have three inspections between now and closing.

Sense 2 needs a plural or a mass noun and no and: between meetings, between semesters, between jobs. It names the empty stretch that falls in the gaps, which is why between jobs is a polite way of saying unemployed. Sense 3 is the everyday planning frame, and it is the one place where between takes a single edge plus the present moment.
examples: The pharmacy is closed between one and two.
I'll call you sometime between Tuesday and Friday.
Between 1994 and 2001, the population doubled.
Between finishing school and starting the job, she spent a summer in Maine.
She grades papers between classes.
The house sat empty between tenants for most of that year.
He wrote three novels between teaching jobs.
There's a lot to do between now and Friday.
Two meetings ran long, and I ate lunch somewhere in between.
Between you and me, the deadline was never real.

entries.pronunciation note: weak /bəˈtwin/
entries.русский: между — промежуток, ограниченный двумя моментами: between 1 and 2 «с часу до двух»
entries.complement: a noun phrase, or the paired frame between [X] and [Y] — the second half must be joined by and, never by or and never by to. Between 2 to 4 is always an error; write between 2 and 4 or from 2 to 4. Gerunds are fine in the paired frame — between finishing school and starting the job — and so is a bare plural or mass noun with no and at all (between meetings). No finite clause: between I got home and dinner is an error, and the repair is a noun phrase on each side. Pronouns take the objective case: between you and me, never between you and I. Between is also an adverb in in between (there's a week in between), where it has no object.
entries.pattern: between [time A] and [time B] · between [verb-ing] and [verb-ing] · between [plural noun phrase] · between now and [future time] · in between [noun phrase] · somewhere between [A] and [B]
entries.variants: betwixt (archaic and dialectal; alive only in betwixt and between), 'tween (poetic)
entries.contrast: Between vs. among: the old rule that between is only for two is a myth — between is correct for any number of individually named points (between 1990, 1995, and 2000), and among is for an undifferentiated mass viewed collectively (among the war years). In time expressions among is almost never right. Between … and vs. from … to: from 2 to 4 is a run you occupy, between 2 and 4 is a window with slack in it — I'll call between 2 and 4 promises one call, not two hours of talking. Against within: between now and Friday names two edges, within two days measures one interval from now.
entries.see also: during, within, through, from, to

entries.meaning: Locates an event inside a named stretch of time without saying where inside.
examples: The fire alarm went off during the meeting.
Somebody's phone rang twice during the second act.
During the war, she worked in a shipyard.
Nothing much grows here during the winter.
Please hold your questions during the presentation.
During my first year in Chicago, I didn't own a coat.
Three windows broke during the storm.
During the last two minutes, the arena never sat down.

senses.head: At some unspecified point within a period
body: The alarm went off during the meeting.

senses.head: Across the whole of a period, when the verb or the context forces that reading
body: During the war she worked in a shipyard.

Which sense you get is decided by the verb, not by during: a punctual verb (went off, called) gives sense 1, a durative one (worked, lived) gives sense 2. The preposition itself is neutral between them.
examples: The fire alarm went off during the meeting.
Somebody's phone rang twice during the second act.
During the war, she worked in a shipyard.
Nothing much grows here during the winter.
Please hold your questions during the presentation.
During my first year in Chicago, I didn't own a coat.
Three windows broke during the storm.
During the last two minutes, the arena never sat down.

entries.pronunciation note: also /ˈdɜrɪŋ/ · DUR-ing · no weak form — the stressed vowel keeps its quality, so during is always audible
entries.русский: во время, в ходе — внутри названного периода; длительность не измеряет (ср. for)
entries.type: simple (historically the participle of the dead verb dure, "to last")
entries.complement: a noun phrase only — a noun naming a period or an event (during the war, during recess). Never a gerund (during eating is an error for while eating), never a finite clause (during I was there is an error for while I was there), and never a bare measurement of length (during three hours is an error for for three hours). Unlike most of the words in this file, during is only ever a preposition — no adverb, no particle, no conjunction — so it must always have a noun phrase after it and nothing else will do.
entries.pattern: during [the period or event] · During [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause] during [noun phrase] · at some point during [period]
entries.contrast: during vs. for is the big one: during answers when and takes a named period, for answers how long and takes a measured length. It rained during the night (when) against it rained for six hours (how long). during vs. while: while takes a clause. during vs. throughout: throughout insists on the entire span with no gaps, during only says somewhere inside it, which is why he coughed during the concert does not mean he coughed for two hours.
entries.see also: throughout, over, within, through, in the course of, in the middle of, at the time of, for, during (participial), while (conjunction)

entries.meaning: For the whole length of a stated period, start to finish. It is the drafting phrase for an obligation that is coextensive with a term — insurance that runs as long as a lease, a restriction that binds as long as an employment lasts.
examples: The tenant must carry insurance for the duration of the lease.
Power stayed out for the duration of the storm.
The pass road is closed for the duration of the repairs.
He was barred from the building for the duration of the investigation.
For the duration of his term, the second seat stays empty.
The clause binds both parties for the duration of the agreement and two years after.
They boarded up the storefront and moved to Ohio for the duration.

senses.head: For the entire length of a stated term or agreement
body: The tenant must carry insurance for the duration of the lease.

senses.head: For the entire length of an event or a condition
body: Power stayed out for the duration of the storm.

senses.head: In the objectless fixed adverbial, for as long as the present emergency lasts
body: They boarded up the storefront and left for the duration.

Sense 3 is a war fossil. Americans enlisted "for the duration of the war" in 1917 and again in 1941, the object wore off, and what was left was a phrase that assumes everyone knows which emergency is meant. Used today it is either historical or dryly funny.
examples: The tenant must carry insurance for the duration of the lease.
Power stayed out for the duration of the storm.
The pass road is closed for the duration of the repairs.
He was barred from the building for the duration of the investigation.
For the duration of his term, the second seat stays empty.
The clause binds both parties for the duration of the agreement and two years after.
They boarded up the storefront and moved to Ohio for the duration.

entries.pronunciation note: for reduces to /fər/ and of to /əv/ or bare /ə/ — fer thuh duh-RAY-shuhn uh
entries.русский: на весь срок — офиц.: на всю продолжительность договора или события
entries.register: formal — legal, military, insurance, and official
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a period or an event that has a term (the lease, the war, the investigation, his sentence). No gerund — for the duration of eating is not English, and for the duration of the meal is the repair. No finite clause. The phrase also lives with no object at all, as the fixed adverbial for the duration (he was interned for the duration), and there it is not a preposition.
entries.pattern: for the duration of [period or event] · For the duration of [event], [clause] · for the duration (fixed adverbial, no object)
entries.contrast: Against during, which puts something at some point inside a period and says nothing about coverage: he was quiet during the meeting allows him a sentence or two, he was quiet for the duration of the meeting does not. That makes it a near-synonym of throughout; the difference is register and the object, since throughout takes any period at all while for the duration of wants one with a defined term — which is why it belongs to leases, policies, and orders. Against plain for, which takes a measured length: for the duration of three hours is padding for for three hours.
entries.see also: throughout, during, through, for the space of, pending, for

entries.meaning: For a stretch of time of a stated length. The noun space here carries its old sense of an interval of time rather than of room, a sense that survives in a short space, in the space of, and breathing space.
examples: The crowd cried out for the space of two hours and would not be quieted.
He stood in the doorway for the space of a full minute and said nothing.
For the space of three days the ship lay becalmed.
She was gone for the space of an hour and came back soaked.
The fever held the town for the space of a summer.
For the space of a week, no word came from the fort.
They kept the fast for the space of forty days.

senses.head: For a stated length of time — the archaic measuring use
body: The crowd cried out for the space of two hours.

senses.head: In narrative, for a stretch through which nothing changed
body: For the space of a week, no word came.

The two senses are one meaning in two settings: the phrase measures, and older narrative liked it because a measured stretch of nothing happening is easier to feel than a bare for. In modern American prose, write for — and if the point is how fast something happened, write in the space of.
examples: The crowd cried out for the space of two hours and would not be quieted.
He stood in the doorway for the space of a full minute and said nothing.
For the space of three days the ship lay becalmed.
She was gone for the space of an hour and came back soaked.
The fever held the town for the space of a summer.
For the space of a week, no word came from the fort.
They kept the fast for the space of forty days.

entries.pronunciation note: for reduces to /fər/ and of to /əv/ or bare /ə/ — fer thuh SPAYSS uh
entries.русский: устар./книжн. в течение, на протяжении — о длительности в высоком стиле
entries.register: archaic and literary — scripture, eighteenth- and nineteenth-century narrative, and deliberate pastiche
entries.complement: a measured length of time, and nothing else — for the space of three days, for the space of an hour. Not a named period: for the space of the war is not idiomatic, and for the duration of is the phrase for that. No gerund, no finite clause.
entries.pattern: for the space of [measured length] · [clause] for the space of [measured length] · For the space of [measured length], [clause]
entries.variants: by the space of and about the space of (both in older biblical English), in the space of (a live modern phrase with a different meaning — see the contrast below)
entries.contrast: It is plain for with three extra words, and the extra words buy period flavor and nothing else: for the space of three days and for three days say exactly the same thing. A modern American meets it in scripture, in Defoe and Scott, and in writing imitating them. Do not confuse it with in the space of, which is alive and means something different — in the space of a year stresses how little time something took (the whole thing collapsed in the space of a year), where for the space of a year merely measures one out.
entries.see also: for the duration of, during, throughout, ere, for

entries.meaning: Somewhere inside a process or a stretch that is under way. The image is the older sense of course — a run, a path traveled — so the phrase suits things that unfold: an investigation, a career, a negotiation, an illness.
examples: In the course of the investigation, two more accounts turned up.
In the course of reviewing the file, she found the missing page.
Nothing like it came up again in the course of his career.
The injury occurred in the course of employment, which is why the claim was paid.
Attendance doubled over the course of three seasons.
Over the course of six months, the debt was paid off entirely.
In the course of a single afternoon the whole plan fell apart.

senses.head: At some point inside a process already under way
body: In the course of the audit, two more accounts turned up.

senses.head: With a gerund, while doing something
body: In the course of reviewing the file, she found the missing page.

senses.head: Across a measured span, in the frame over the course of
body: Attendance doubled over the course of three seasons.

Sense 3 is where the phrase is genuinely useful in ordinary prose: over the course of spreads a change out along a span in a way that bare over leaves flat. Sense 1 is the one to cut whenever during will do the same work.
examples: In the course of the investigation, two more accounts turned up.
In the course of reviewing the file, she found the missing page.
Nothing like it came up again in the course of his career.
The injury occurred in the course of employment, which is why the claim was paid.
Attendance doubled over the course of three seasons.
Over the course of six months, the debt was paid off entirely.
In the course of a single afternoon the whole plan fell apart.

entries.pronunciation note: of reduces to /əv/ or bare /ə/ — in thuh KORSS uh
entries.русский: в ходе, в течение — офиц.: в какой-то момент внутри идущего процесса
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a process or a stretch (in the course of the investigation), or a gerund (in the course of reviewing the file) — never a finite clause. The gerund is the whole reason to keep the phrase: during refuses one, so during reviewing the file is an error and in the course of reviewing the file is the repair.
entries.pattern: in the course of [process noun] · in the course of [verb-ing] · In the course of [noun phrase], [clause] · over the course of [measured span] · in the ordinary course of [business]
entries.variants: over the course of (the commoner form with a measured span — over the course of three years), during the course of (redundant; editors cut the course of and leave during), in the ordinary course and in the course of employment (fixed legal phrases that cannot be shortened)
entries.contrast: In the course of and during both put something inside a stretch, and during is three syllables shorter — which is why usage guides call the longer phrase padding. It earns its place in exactly two spots: in front of a gerund, where during cannot go, and in in the course of employment, where a whole doctrine of workplace liability hangs on the words. Against over the course of: in prefers a process (in the course of the audit), over prefers a measured span (over the course of six months). Against throughout, which claims every moment of the span: in the course of claims only some moment in it.
entries.see also: during, throughout, over, within, in the middle of, at the time of, for

entries.meaning: Inside a period or an activity already under way, most often at the moment something cuts in. Literal centering is rare — in the middle of the night is any dark hour, not 12:00 sharp.
examples: The phone rang in the middle of the night.
He walked out in the middle of the ceremony.
We lost power right in the middle of dinner.
I was in the middle of eating when they knocked.
She's in the middle of moving and can't find anything.
In the middle of all this, the landlord raised the rent.
Don't call me in the middle of the workday unless something is on fire.

senses.head: At some point inside a period, characteristically an inconvenient one
body: The phone rang in the middle of the night.

senses.head: Inside an activity already under way, with a noun
body: He walked out in the middle of the ceremony.

senses.head: With a gerund, in the act of doing something
body: I was in the middle of eating when they knocked.

Sense 3 is the one worth drilling. During eating is an error and while eating is the textbook repair, but what Americans actually say is in the middle of eating — and unlike while, it needs no subject and no tense.
examples: The phone rang in the middle of the night.
He walked out in the middle of the ceremony.
We lost power right in the middle of dinner.
I was in the middle of eating when they knocked.
She's in the middle of moving and can't find anything.
In the middle of all this, the landlord raised the rent.
Don't call me in the middle of the workday unless something is on fire.

entries.pronunciation note: of reduces to /əv/ or bare /ə/, and in fast speech the tail flattens to a single syllable — in thuh MIDD-luh
entries.русский: посреди, в середине — разг.: внутри периода или занятия, часто некстати
entries.register: neutral to informal — the everyday spoken form
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a period or an activity (in the middle of the night, in the middle of dinner) or a gerund (in the middle of eating, in the middle of moving) — never a finite clause. In the middle of I was eating is an error and the gerund is the repair. That gerund is what makes this the everyday spoken substitute for while, and it is the reason during eating has an idiomatic fix at all.
entries.pattern: in the middle of [period] · in the middle of [activity noun] · in the middle of [verb-ing] · right in the middle of [noun phrase] · be in the middle of [something]
entries.contrast: Against during, which takes a noun phrase and stops there: during dinner and in the middle of dinner both work, but only the second can carry on into a verb — in the middle of eating dinner. Against halfway through, which actually measures: halfway through the movie is a position on the clock, in the middle of the movie usually means only "while it was running, at a bad moment." Against at the time of, which is neutral: this phrase almost always brings interruption with it.
entries.see also: during, through, at the time of, in the course of, into, in

entries.meaning: Carries an activity across the edge of a period and keeps it going inside — or measures how far inside a period something happened.
examples: They argued into the night and settled nothing.
The renovation dragged on into a second winter.
The party ran late into Sunday morning.
Ten minutes into the flight, an engine light came on.
Three weeks into the semester, half the class had dropped.
Twenty minutes into filming, the generator quit.
Two years into running the shop, she still opens it herself.
She kept teaching well into her eighties.
The drought stretched far into the following spring.

senses.head: Continuing past a boundary and on into a period
body: The argument went on into the night.

senses.head: At a stated distance inside a period already under way
body: Ten minutes into the flight, an engine light came on.

senses.head: Deep inside a long stretch or a stage of life, with well, far, or deep
body: She kept teaching well into her eighties.

Sense 1 almost always carries a note of excess or persistence — you work into the night, not into the afternoon. Sense 2 is a measuring use and is perfectly neutral; it is the standard American way to time-stamp something inside an event, and it is why sportscasters say four minutes into the third quarter. Sense 3 needs its extent adverb: into his eighties alone is odd, well into his eighties is idiomatic.
examples: They argued into the night and settled nothing.
The renovation dragged on into a second winter.
The party ran late into Sunday morning.
Ten minutes into the flight, an engine light came on.
Three weeks into the semester, half the class had dropped.
Twenty minutes into filming, the generator quit.
Two years into running the shop, she still opens it herself.
She kept teaching well into her eighties.
The drought stretched far into the following spring.

entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˈɪntə/ before a consonant · IN-tuh; casual /ˈɪnə/ · IN-uh
entries.русский: вплоть до, вглубь периода — продолжение за границу: into the night «до глубокой ночи»
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a period, nearly always with a modifier of extent in front of it (far into the night, well into his eighties, three weeks into the semester). After a measure phrase a gerund is idiomatic too — ten minutes into filming, two years into running the shop. No finite clause: into he arrived is not English. Note that into is only ever a preposition; it has no adverb or particle use, which is what separates it from bare in — come in is the adverb with no object, while come into the room still has one and is the preposition.
entries.pattern: [verb] into [the period] · far, well, deep, or late into [the period] · [measure phrase] into [period] · [measure phrase] into [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: in vs. into is the contrast to memorize here. In locates something inside a period; into adds motion, carrying the event across a boundary and onward — they talked in the night is a location, they talked into the night is a trespass past bedtime. Against through: through the night covers the night end to end, into the night only says the activity kept going past the point where it should have stopped. Against within: three weeks into the semester counts forward from the semester's start, within three weeks counts forward from now. The movement senses (into the room) live in into.
entries.see also: through, until, over, beyond, in the middle of, in, into (movement)

entries.meaning: Spreads an event across a stretch of time that the speaker is looking at whole, from the outside. Every sense below is that same image applied to a different kind of stretch: a season, a measured run of years, a meal, a quantity, or an illness.
examples: We're driving to Duluth over the long weekend.
The shop stays open over the holidays.
Enrollment dropped sharply over the last five years.
Over the past decade the neighborhood has turned completely.
They worked out the whole deal over coffee.
She told me over dinner that she was quitting.
We hashed it out over the phone instead of flying anybody in.
The outage lasted over an hour.
He's been with the company over twenty years.
She was over the flu by Thursday and back at work Friday.
He said he was over it, and for once he sounded like he meant it.

senses.head: Across the whole of a named period, viewed as a span
body: We're driving to Duluth over the long weekend.

senses.head: Across a measured stretch counted back from now, in the frame over the past / last [quantity]
body: Attendance fell over the last five years.

senses.head: In the course of an activity, especially a meal, or by way of a medium
body: We settled it over coffee.

senses.head: More than, with a quantity of time
body: The delay lasted over an hour.

senses.head: Finished with, past the worst of — with an illness, a feeling, or a person
body: She's over the flu.

Sense 3 is the one learners miss. Over dinner does not mean above the food; it means the conversation and the dinner occupied the same stretch, which is why over drinks, over lunch, and over the phone all work the same way. Sense 5 is the same reach-across image applied to a condition rather than a clock, and it is the sense that produces the flat American I'm over it.
examples: We're driving to Duluth over the long weekend.
The shop stays open over the holidays.
Enrollment dropped sharply over the last five years.
Over the past decade the neighborhood has turned completely.
They worked out the whole deal over coffee.
She told me over dinner that she was quitting.
We hashed it out over the phone instead of flying anybody in.
The outage lasted over an hour.
He's been with the company over twenty years.
She was over the flu by Thursday and back at work Friday.
He said he was over it, and for once he sounded like he meant it.

entries.pronunciation note: no weak form — the second syllable is already a reduced /ɚ/ and the first keeps its diphthong; the poetic contraction o'er /ɔr/ is dead outside verse
entries.русский: в течение, за — о периоде целиком: over the weekend «за выходные»; также «свыше» о сроке
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a period (over the summer), an activity or a meal (over lunch), a medium (over the phone), a quantity of time (over an hour), or a condition being left behind (over the flu). No finite clause, and no gerund — over eating is not this preposition but the compound verb overeating, a different word. The one place a gerund turns up nearby is the frame over the course of writing it, where the gerund is the object of of and not of over at all. Over is also an adverb (it's over, come over), an adjective (the game is over), and a verb particle (think it over, the car flipped over); the preposition has an object and the adverb does not — compare the meeting is over with we talked it out over lunch.
entries.pattern: over [the period] · over the past / last [measured stretch] · over [meal, activity, or medium] · over [quantity of time] · over the course of [period] · be over [an illness or a feeling]
entries.contrast: Over vs. during: over prefers a span you survey from outside, especially a recent one (over the past decade), while during prefers a named event. Over vs. through: over the weekend surveys the span from outside, through the weekend runs it end to end without a gap. Over vs. for: over three hours means "more than," for three hours means "that long"; the opposite of that over is under (in under an hour). Over the weekend and on the weekend are standard American; British at the weekend is not.
entries.see also: during, throughout, through, within, beyond, past, in the course of, for, over (movement)

entries.meaning: Runs an event along a stretch of time from one end to the other — and, in the American range use, includes the far end.
examples: The clinic is open Monday through Friday.
Tickets are on sale through the end of March.
The exhibit runs June 3 through September 12.
Coverage lasts through December 31 and not a day longer.
He slept all through the second half.
She practiced through the whole summer without a break.
We kept the shop open through the holidays.
We left halfway through the second act.
Partway through cooking dinner, the power went out.
She got through the winter on savings and a lot of soup.

senses.head: Up to and including the stated endpoint of a range
body: The office is open Monday through Friday.

senses.head: From the beginning to the end of a period, with no gaps
body: He slept all through the movie.

senses.head: At a measured distance inside an activity, with halfway, partway, or a fraction
body: We left halfway through the second act.

senses.head: Out the far side of a hard stretch, usually with get, make it, or come
body: She got through the winter on savings.

Sense 1 is the workhorse, and it is why American schedules, store hours, and government notices are less ambiguous than British ones. Sense 2 usually wants all in front of it and overlaps with throughout. Sense 4 always implies difficulty: you get through a winter, a diagnosis, or a divorce, not through a vacation.
examples: The clinic is open Monday through Friday.
Tickets are on sale through the end of March.
The exhibit runs June 3 through September 12.
Coverage lasts through December 31 and not a day longer.
He slept all through the second half.
She practiced through the whole summer without a break.
We kept the shop open through the holidays.
We left halfway through the second act.
Partway through cooking dinner, the power went out.
She got through the winter on savings and a lot of soup.

entries.pronunciation note: weak /θrə/ before a consonant in fast speech — thruh (through the door → /θrə ðə dɔr/)
entries.русский: по … включительно; на протяжении — Monday through Friday «с понедельника по пятницу»
entries.complement: a noun phrase: a day, a date, a period, or the second element of a range. After a measure phrase it also takes a gerund — halfway through cooking dinner, partway through reading it. No finite clause: through the movie ended is not English. Through is also an adverb (let me through), a predicative adjective (I'm through with it), and a verb particle (see it through); the preposition takes an object and the adverb does not — compare we're through with we're through Friday.
entries.pattern: [start] through [end] · from [start] through [end] · all through [period] · through [period] · halfway or partway through [period or verb-ing] · get through [a hard stretch]
entries.variants: thru (informal spelling — signs, notes, and menus only, never in prose)
entries.contrast: This is the American inclusive-endpoint word, and it is one of the clearest AmE/BrE differences in the language. Monday through Friday includes Friday. British English writes Monday to Friday, which many Americans read as possibly stopping at the start of Friday. Against till and until, which stop at the boundary rather than including it: open until Friday is genuinely ambiguous, open through Friday is not. Against throughout, which claims the whole span emphatically and takes no range: there is no Monday throughout Friday. In contracts the belt-and-suspenders form is up to and including. The path senses (through the tunnel) live in through.
entries.see also: throughout, until, till, up to, between, no later than, to

entries.meaning: For the whole of a period, from one end to the other, without interruption. The word is emphatic by construction — through plus out — so it is wasted on short spans: throughout the afternoon is normal, throughout the minute is not.
examples: It rained throughout the weekend.
Throughout the 1970s, the plant ran three shifts.
She stayed calm throughout the entire ordeal.
Prices held steady throughout the year.
Throughout his presidency, the same three advisers kept their jobs.
The baby cried throughout the flight.
Interruptions came throughout the hearing, and the chair finally cleared the room.
The same warning is repeated throughout the manual.

senses.head: For the whole of a period, with a state that holds without a break
body: It rained throughout the weekend.

senses.head: At every point across a period, with events that keep recurring
body: Interruptions came throughout the hearing.

senses.head: Everywhere inside a place — the spatial sense, listed here only so the split is visible
body: The company has offices throughout the Southwest.

Senses 1 and 2 are the same claim of total coverage seen from two angles: sense 1 says a condition never lapsed, sense 2 says events kept coming and no stretch was spared. The verb picks the sense — a stative verb (rained, held, stayed) gives 1, a countable event (came, cried out, rang) gives 2. Sense 3 belongs with the place prepositions and has its own entry there.
examples: It rained throughout the weekend.
Throughout the 1970s, the plant ran three shifts.
She stayed calm throughout the entire ordeal.
Prices held steady throughout the year.
Throughout his presidency, the same three advisers kept their jobs.
The baby cried throughout the flight.
Interruptions came throughout the hearing, and the chair finally cleared the room.
The same warning is repeated throughout the manual.

entries.pronunciation note: weak first syllable /θrəˈaʊt/ · thruh-OWT — the stress is always on -out
entries.русский: на протяжении всего, всё время — без перерывов через весь период
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a period (or, in the spatial sense, a place). No gerund, no finite clause. It is also an adverb with no object at all (the mood stayed tense throughout), and that stranded use is common — the preposition has an object, the adverb ends the clause bare.
entries.pattern: throughout [the period] · Throughout [period], [clause] · [clause] throughout (adverb, no object)
entries.contrast: Throughout vs. during: throughout claims the entire span with no gaps, during is silent about coverage. He was quiet during the meeting allows him a sentence or two; he was quiet throughout the meeting does not. Throughout vs. all through: same meaning, and all through is the plainer, more spoken form.
entries.see also: during, through, over, within, in the course of, throughout (movement)

entries.meaning: Draws a boundary and puts the event inside it, before the far edge is reached. Everything within does is about a limit not crossed, which is why it is the deadline word of American contracts, warranties, statutes, and return policies.
examples: Please reply within forty-eight hours.
The package should arrive within three business days.
He was back on his feet within a month.
Cancel within thirty days and the fee is refunded in full.
She died within a week of her husband.
The lawsuit has to be filed within two years of the injury.
Within the fiscal year, the department has to spend it or lose it.
Within the first two weeks of the session, every bill has to be introduced.

senses.head: Before a stated amount of time has elapsed
body: Reply within 48 hours.

senses.head: Not more than a stated distance in time from some other event
body: She died within a week of her husband.

senses.head: At some point inside a bounded named period
body: Within the fiscal year, the department has to spend it or lose it.

Sense 2 works in both directions — within a week of the wedding can be the week before or the week after, and only context settles it. Sense 3 comes closest to plain in, and it survives as a separate sense only because a fiscal year, a term, or a legislative session has hard edges to be inside of.
examples: Please reply within forty-eight hours.
The package should arrive within three business days.
He was back on his feet within a month.
Cancel within thirty days and the fee is refunded in full.
She died within a week of her husband.
The lawsuit has to be filed within two years of the injury.
Within the fiscal year, the department has to spend it or lose it.
Within the first two weeks of the session, every bill has to be introduced.

entries.pronunciation note: weak /wəˈðɪn/ — the th is voiced, as in this
entries.русский: в пределах, не позднее чем через — within 48 hours «в течение 48 часов»
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a length of time (within an hour) or a bounded period (within the fiscal year); also the frame within [length] of [event]. No gerund directly after within — but the of-frame takes one freely, since the gerund there is the object of of: within a week of moving in. No finite clause. In literary use within is also an adverb or a noun (a voice from within), where it has no object.
entries.pattern: within [length of time] · within [length] of [event] · within [the bounded period]
entries.contrast: in vs. within is the contrast worth memorizing. I'll be there in an hour means at the end of the hour — sixty minutes from now. I'll be there within an hour means at any point before the hour is up. For a deadline, within is the unambiguous word and in is not. Informal American also says inside of an hour for exactly the within meaning. Against by: by noon fixes a clock time, within two hours fixes an interval measured from now.
entries.see also: during, up to, until, no later than, in the course of, in, by, inside of

entries.meaning: Earlier than a point that was already fixed. The word doing the work is already: there has to be a schedule, a due date, or a scheduled event for something to be ahead of, which is exactly the restriction plain before does not have.
examples: The bridge reopened three months ahead of schedule.
Pay the invoice ahead of the due date and you get two percent off.
Call me ahead of time if you're bringing anyone.
Traders sold off ahead of the Fed announcement.
Ahead of Tuesday's hearing, both sides filed briefs.
She resigned ahead of being formally charged.
Ahead of the holiday weekend, every flight out was already full.

senses.head: Earlier than a scheduled or expected point
body: The bridge opened three months ahead of schedule.

senses.head: In the period leading up to an event
body: Traders sold off ahead of the Fed announcement.

Sense 1 is old and universal. Sense 2 is newer, is everywhere in journalism, and is the one to use sparingly: before the vote says the same thing without sounding like a wire report. The same newsroom slot is filled by on the eve of when the writer wants drama and by in advance of when the point is preparation.
examples: The bridge reopened three months ahead of schedule.
Pay the invoice ahead of the due date and you get two percent off.
Call me ahead of time if you're bringing anyone.
Traders sold off ahead of the Fed announcement.
Ahead of Tuesday's hearing, both sides filed briefs.
She resigned ahead of being formally charged.
Ahead of the holiday weekend, every flight out was already full.

entries.pronunciation note: of reduces to /əv/ or /ə/ — uh-HED uh
entries.русский: раньше, накануне — раньше срока (ahead of schedule) или в преддверии события
entries.complement: a noun phrase or a gerund (ahead of signing the deal) — never a finite clause. The fixed forms ahead of schedule and ahead of time take no article.
entries.pattern: ahead of [noun phrase] · ahead of [verb-ing] · ahead of schedule, ahead of time · Ahead of [event], [clause]
entries.contrast: Against plain before: ahead of adds either "earlier than the plan called for" (ahead of schedule) or the newsroom sense "in the run-up to" (ahead of Tuesday's vote), which has spread fast since about 2000 and which some editors still resist. Note that ahead of time is idiomatic and before time is not English. The opposite is behind.
entries.see also: before, prior to, in advance of, on the eve of, behind, by, ahead of (complex)

entries.meaning: States the date at which a figure or a state of affairs is measured. It is the standard heading language of accounts prepared under IFRS and under UK, Canadian, Australian, and Indian practice — Statement of Financial Position as at 31 December — and an American meets it in a cross-border audit report, a foreign subsidiary's accounts, an IFRS filing, or a contract drafted in London.
examples: Cash and equivalents as at December 31 were $4.2 million.
The statement of financial position as at 31 March 2025 was signed by two directors.
The register of members as at the date of this notice lists forty-one names.
Inventory as at year end had already been written down twice.
Head count as at the reporting date was 1,180.
The valuation was prepared as at the last day of the quarter.
As at the close of business Friday, the account was still overdrawn.

senses.head: Measured at a stated reporting date — the accounting use
body: Cash as at December 31 was $4.2 million.

senses.head: As things stood at a stated date, in official and legal prose more generally
body: The register as at the date of this notice lists forty-one members.

American practice writes as of for both. Recognize as at, leave it alone when you are editing an IFRS statement to house style, and do not import it into American copy — to an American ear it reads as a typo for as of.
examples: Cash and equivalents as at December 31 were $4.2 million.
The statement of financial position as at 31 March 2025 was signed by two directors.
The register of members as at the date of this notice lists forty-one names.
Inventory as at year end had already been written down twice.
Head count as at the reporting date was 1,180.
The valuation was prepared as at the last day of the quarter.
As at the close of business Friday, the account was still overdrawn.

entries.pronunciation note: weak /əz ət/ — uhz uht; both words reduce, so in speech the phrase is nearly a single unstressed foot
entries.русский: по состоянию на — брит./бухг.: на отчётную дату; в амер. английском пишут as of
entries.register: formal — chiefly British and Commonwealth accounting; in American English a foreign-office usage to recognize, not to write
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a date, characteristically a reporting date (as at 31 December 2024, as at the balance sheet date, as at year end). No clock time in ordinary use, no gerund, no finite clause. It cannot look forward: there is no as at July 1 the rate goes up, and that is the one grammatical difference from as of.
entries.pattern: as at [date] · [figure] as at [date] · as at the balance sheet date · as at year end
entries.contrast: The American equivalent is as of, and an American should write as of. The two are not fully interchangeable even in Britain: as at is a snapshot and looks only backward, while as of does that and can point forward to a change taking force. As at December 31 reports a balance; as of January 1 can announce a new rate. Against with effect from and as from, which are the forward-facing Commonwealth phrases — the trio splits neatly, as at backward, as from and with effect from forward.
entries.see also: as of, as from, with effect from, effective, at the time of

entries.meaning: Starting on a stated date. It announces that something takes force from that date onward, and it belongs to British and Commonwealth contracts, employment letters, and official notices.
examples: As from September 1, the office closes at four.
Her salary is increased as from January 1, and the arrears will be paid this month.
As from the date of this letter, you are no longer authorized to sign for the company.
The tariff applies as from the first shipment of the year.
As from next term, the fee covers materials.
The lease runs for five years as from the commencement date.
As from Monday, all deliveries go to the rear entrance.

senses.head: Taking force from a stated future date
body: As from September 1, the office closes at four.

senses.head: Backdated — taking force from a stated past date
body: Her salary is increased as from January 1.

Sense 2 is the one that carries money. A raise as from a date already past is a backdated raise, and arrears follow; American letters say effective January 1 or retroactive to January 1 and mean the same thing.
examples: As from September 1, the office closes at four.
Her salary is increased as from January 1, and the arrears will be paid this month.
As from the date of this letter, you are no longer authorized to sign for the company.
The tariff applies as from the first shipment of the year.
As from next term, the fee covers materials.
The lease runs for five years as from the commencement date.
As from Monday, all deliveries go to the rear entrance.

entries.pronunciation note: weak /əz frəm/ — uhz fruhm; in running speech both words reduce and the stress lands on the date
entries.русский: начиная с — брит. офиц.: с указанной даты; амер. эквивалент — as of
entries.register: formal — chiefly British and Commonwealth; in American English a Britishism to recognize, not to write
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a date or a starting point (as from July 1, as from the date of this letter, as from the commencement date). No gerund, no finite clause. It looks forward only: as from starts a clock, so there is no as from last year we had four hundred orders.
entries.pattern: As from [date], [clause] · [clause] as from [date] · as from the date of [document]
entries.contrast: The American forms are as of and effective: as of July 1, the rate goes up, or effective July 1, the rate goes up. British drafting also uses with effect from, which is the same idea at greater length. Against as at, the backward-looking snapshot: as from opens a period, as at reads one. Against plain from, which does the same job in every register and is what most British writers now use anyway — the as adds only officialness.
entries.see also: as of, as at, with effect from, effective, from and after, from, starting

entries.meaning: Names a date and pins a statement to it. Which way the sentence points — forward to a change or backward to a state — is decided by the tense of the verb, not by as of, and that is why the phrase can do both jobs with the same two words.
examples: As of Monday, masks are optional in the building.
As of January 1, the deposit goes up to two hundred dollars.
As of Friday, we had 412 registrations.
The account balance as of yesterday's close was negative.
As of this writing, no arrests have been made.
She is, as of last month, the longest-serving member of the board.
As of six o'clock, the roads through the pass were still closed.

senses.head: Starting from a stated date, looking forward
body: As of Monday, masks are optional.

senses.head: Measured at a stated date, as a snapshot, looking backward
body: As of Friday, we had 412 registrations.

The forward sense is an announcement; the backward sense is a reading off a meter. Sense 2 is why as of this writing and as of now are so useful — they date a claim without committing the writer to what happens next.
examples: As of Monday, masks are optional in the building.
As of January 1, the deposit goes up to two hundred dollars.
As of Friday, we had 412 registrations.
The account balance as of yesterday's close was negative.
As of this writing, no arrests have been made.
She is, as of last month, the longest-serving member of the board.
As of six o'clock, the roads through the pass were still closed.

entries.pronunciation note: weak /əz əv/ or /əz ə/ — uhz uh
entries.русский: с, по состоянию на — с указанной даты вперёд или на указанную дату как срез
entries.register: neutral to formal — business, legal, journalistic
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a date or a time point (as of Monday, as of this writing, as of yesterday's close). No gerund, no clause.
entries.pattern: As of [date], [clause] · [clause] as of [date] · as of [date], [figure]
entries.variants: as from (British; Americans write as of or effective), as at (British accounting, for a balance-sheet date)
entries.contrast: As of looks both directions, and that is its whole trick. Pointed forward it announces a change that takes force at that moment (as of July 1, the rate goes up); pointed backward it reports the state of things at that moment (as of Friday, 400 tickets were left). Effective can only do the first. Since opens a stretch; as of names its edge and says nothing about what follows.
entries.see also: effective, as at, as from, with effect from, since, up to, upon, from, starting, beginning

entries.meaning: Puts something later than the standard it is being measured against — the mirror of ahead of. Like ahead of, it needs a plan, a clock, or a competitor for the lateness to be measured from; there is no behind in the abstract.
examples: The project is running six weeks behind schedule.
We fell behind schedule the day the inspector showed up.
The train pulled in twenty minutes behind schedule. (British copy would say behind time.)
He's a full lap behind the leader.
Her fundraising is behind where it was at this point last cycle.
All of that is behind us now.
Two more weeks and the whole audit is behind us.
She's behind on rent for the second month in a row.
He's badly behind on filing his quarterly reports.

senses.head: Later than a plan or a schedule required
body: The project is six weeks behind schedule.

senses.head: Trailing a competitor at a given moment
body: He's a full lap behind the leader.

senses.head: In the past and finished with, from the speaker's point of view
body: Those years are behind us now.
Sense 3 always has the period as subject and a form of be — the worst is behind us — and it carries a note of relief that the neutral in the past does not.
examples: The project is running six weeks behind schedule.
We fell behind schedule the day the inspector showed up.
The train pulled in twenty minutes behind schedule. (British copy would say behind time.)
He's a full lap behind the leader.
Her fundraising is behind where it was at this point last cycle.
All of that is behind us now.
Two more weeks and the whole audit is behind us.
She's behind on rent for the second month in a row.
He's badly behind on filing his quarterly reports.

entries.pronunciation note: weak /bəˈhaɪnd/
entries.русский: позади, с отставанием от — отставая от графика или соперника; также «в прошлом»
entries.complement: in the temporal sense, a small and mostly fixed set of noun phrases — schedule, time, plan, or a competitor (behind the leader). Related but distinct is behind on + an obligation, where on is required and the object may be a noun or a gerund: behind on rent, behind on filing her taxes. No gerund directly after bare behind, and no finite clause. Behind is also an adverb (he stayed behind, we fell behind), a noun, and a place preposition; the preposition has an object and the adverb does not — compare we fell behind with we fell behind schedule.
entries.pattern: behind schedule · run, fall, or get behind [noun phrase] · behind [competitor] · behind on [obligation]
entries.variants: behind time (chiefly British; American English says behind schedule)
entries.contrast: The mirror of ahead of. Do not confuse the schedule sense with the place sense (behind the garage) or with behind the times, which means old-fashioned rather than late. Against past: past the deadline says the wall has been crossed, behind schedule says you are losing ground against a plan that is still running.
entries.see also: ahead of, past, after, beyond, over

entries.meaning: Puts an event on the far side of a limit, with the limit still in view. Where after names a later time and says nothing about it, beyond implies that the time it names was supposed to be an end.
examples: The talks went on beyond midnight.
Nothing on the schedule extends beyond Friday.
The lease runs beyond the end of the fiscal year.
He stayed at the paper well beyond retirement age.
Coverage does not continue beyond the warranty period.
By two in the morning she was beyond caring who won.
The car was beyond saving after the second winter.

senses.head: Later than a stated time or limit
body: The talks went on beyond midnight.

senses.head: Longer than a period was meant to last
body: Nothing on the schedule extends beyond Friday.

senses.head: Past the point of, in a closed set of idioms
body: By then she was beyond caring.

Sense 3 is the evaluative one and it is always about exhaustion or ruin: beyond help, beyond repair, beyond saving, beyond caring. It is the same reach-past-a-limit image as sense 1 applied to a condition instead of a clock.
examples: The talks went on beyond midnight.
Nothing on the schedule extends beyond Friday.
The lease runs beyond the end of the fiscal year.
He stayed at the paper well beyond retirement age.
Coverage does not continue beyond the warranty period.
By two in the morning she was beyond caring who won.
The car was beyond saving after the second winter.

entries.pronunciation note: weak /bəˈjɑnd/ · buh-YAHND
entries.русский: за пределами, после — позже указанного времени или предела: beyond midnight «за полночь»
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a point in time or a limit; a gerund only in a closed set of idioms (beyond caring, beyond saving, beyond repairing). Never a clause. Beyond is also an adverb (the fields beyond) and a noun (the great beyond); the preposition has an object and the adverb does not — compare the years beyond with beyond the next two years. The spatial senses belong with the place prepositions.
entries.pattern: beyond [point in time] · beyond [a stated limit] · go, run, stretch, or extend beyond [time] · beyond [verb-ing] (closed set) · well beyond [time]
entries.contrast: Beyond midnight and past midnight both report a line crossed; beyond is the more literary of the two and is likelier when the crossing is unwelcome, surprising, or beyond anyone's plan. Against after, which is neutral about limits: the meeting ran beyond six says six was supposed to be the end, and the meeting ran after six is not idiomatic at all. Against over: over an hour counts a quantity, beyond an hour pushes past a stated ceiling.
entries.see also: past, after, over, into, until

entries.meaning: Names a period and makes its far edge the deadline. The action may land anywhere inside the period; what the phrase forbids is landing outside it.
examples: Have the draft to me by the end of the week.
The permits have to be filed by the end of the quarter.
By the end of the day, everybody had heard some version of it.
We should know by the end of the month whether the grant came through.
By the end of the trial, three jurors had been replaced.
By the end of the first winter, half the settlers were gone.
Get me an answer by the end of business Friday.

senses.head: On or before the last moment of a stated period — a deadline
body: Have the draft to me by the end of the week.

senses.head: By the time a process has run its course — a vantage point rather than a deadline
body: By the end of the trial, three jurors had been replaced.

Sense 2 is not a deadline at all, and it is worth separating because it changes the tense: it looks back from the far edge and takes the past perfect — by the end of the war, half the town had moved away. Sense 1 looks forward and takes a plain future or an imperative.
examples: Have the draft to me by the end of the week.
The permits have to be filed by the end of the quarter.
By the end of the day, everybody had heard some version of it.
We should know by the end of the month whether the grant came through.
By the end of the trial, three jurors had been replaced.
By the end of the first winter, half the settlers were gone.
Get me an answer by the end of business Friday.

entries.pronunciation note: by has no weak form of its own and keeps /baɪ/ even unstressed; the is /ði/ before the vowel of end, and of reduces to /əv/ or bare /ə/ — by thee END uh
entries.русский: к концу — не позже последнего момента периода: by the end of the week «к концу недели»
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a period or a process (the week, the quarter, the trial). No gerund — by the end of eating is not English. No finite clause. The article is fixed.
entries.pattern: by the end of [period] · By the end of [period], [clause] · by the end of the day · by the end of business [Friday]
entries.variants: by close of business and by COB (the office abbreviation), by the close of [period] (formal)
entries.contrast: This is at the end of turned into a deadline, and the two are not interchangeable. At the end of the month names the last day; by the end of the month names the last acceptable day and takes any earlier one. It inherits everything from by: a punctual verb (file, finish, pay), a completed action, and no claim about what happens afterward. Against before the end of, which excludes the last day and is a day tighter. Against no later than, which is the same deadline in contract dress, and within, which measures an interval from now instead of naming a period.
entries.see also: at the end of, no later than, on or before, within, until, by

entries.meaning: Beginning on the stated date and continuing thereafter. The phrase marks the moment an obligation, a title, or a rule starts to run, and the doubled words are there to make the starting day itself unarguable. An American meets it in a deed, a bond indenture, the effective-date clause of an ordinance, and the transition provisions of a state statute.
examples: Interest accrues on the unpaid balance from and after the Closing Date.
From and after the effective date of this ordinance, no permit shall issue for such use.
The covenants run with the land from and after the recording of this deed.
Buyer assumes all liabilities from and after the Closing.
Rent shall be payable monthly from and after the Commencement Date.
From and after the date hereof, the guarantor is released.
Coverage applies to claims made from and after the retroactive date.

senses.head: Beginning on a stated date and continuing indefinitely
body: Interest accrues from and after the Closing Date.

senses.head: Beginning at a named event
body: From and after the recording of this deed, the covenants run with the land.

Both senses are one idea: a start line that includes its own day. The reason the doublet survived is that the money question — who owns the interest that accrued on the closing day itself — has actually been litigated, and from alone has lost it.
examples: Interest accrues on the unpaid balance from and after the Closing Date.
From and after the effective date of this ordinance, no permit shall issue for such use.
The covenants run with the land from and after the recording of this deed.
Buyer assumes all liabilities from and after the Closing.
Rent shall be payable monthly from and after the Commencement Date.
From and after the date hereof, the guarantor is released.
Coverage applies to claims made from and after the retroactive date.

entries.pronunciation note: from and and both reduce hard — /frəm ən/ — so the phrase is heard as a single run, frum-un-AF-ter
entries.русский: юр. начиная с и после — дублет в договорах: с указанной даты и далее
entries.register: legal — deeds, indentures, contracts, statutes, and municipal ordinances
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a date or a dated event (from and after the Closing Date, from and after the effective date of this ordinance, from and after the date hereof). No gerund, no finite clause.
entries.pattern: from and after [date] · from and after [named event] · [obligation] from and after [date] · from and after the date hereof
entries.variants: on and after (the same doublet with the same meaning, and three syllables shorter; modern drafting manuals prefer it), from and after the date hereof (the fixed self-referential form)
entries.contrast: It is a doublet — two words doing one word's work, like give and bequeath or null and void — and it exists to close a gap that plain from might be argued to leave open: does a period running from June 1 include June 1? From and after June 1 answers that it starts on June 1 and runs onward. Modern drafting guides call it surplusage and tell you to write on and after or simply beginning. Against as of, which dates a statement rather than starting an obligation running; against with effect from, its Commonwealth cousin; against on or after, which sorts events into a window rather than starting a clock.
entries.see also: on or after, as of, as from, with effect from, effective, from

entries.meaning: In the stated month, season, or year, or near enough to it that the difference is immaterial. Like on or about, it exists to keep an allegation alive when a witness's memory is imprecise, and it is a fixture of American charging documents and civil complaints.
examples: In or about March 2018, the defendant opened an account in a false name.
The complaint alleges that the payments stopped in or about the fall of 2020.
She was hired in or about January 2016 and terminated two years later.
In or about 1997, the company began storing the drums behind the plant.
The witness recalls a conversation in or about the week of the storm.
Defendant resided at that address in or about the period charged in Count Two.
The parties began negotiating in or about the summer, though nobody wrote anything down.

senses.head: In a stated month or year, or near it — the pleading use
body: In or about March 2018, the defendant opened the account.

senses.head: In a stated season or vague stretch
body: The payments stopped in or about the fall of 2020.

The hedge runs both directions and has no stated width, which is exactly what a pleader wants and exactly what makes the phrase useless outside a legal document. Written anywhere else it reads as evasion rather than as care.
examples: In or about March 2018, the defendant opened an account in a false name.
The complaint alleges that the payments stopped in or about the fall of 2020.
She was hired in or about January 2016 and terminated two years later.
In or about 1997, the company began storing the drums behind the plant.
The witness recalls a conversation in or about the week of the storm.
Defendant resided at that address in or about the period charged in Count Two.
The parties began negotiating in or about the summer, though nobody wrote anything down.

entries.pronunciation note: or reduces to /ər/ and in takes no stress, so the phrase runs together as in-er-uh-BOWT
entries.русский: юр. в или около — в указанном месяце или году либо примерно в это время
entries.register: legal — pleadings, indictments, affidavits, and investigative reports
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a stretch rather than a day: a month, a season, a year, or a vague period (in or about June 2019, in or about the summer of 2020). No gerund, no finite clause. The same documents use the phrase of place as well (in or about the vehicle), which is a different sense of in and not a time expression at all.
entries.pattern: in or about [month and year] · in or about [year] · in or about [the season or period] · [clause] in or about [period]
entries.contrast: It is the period-sized twin of on or about, and the two split by the object: on or about takes a date (on or about June 3), in or about takes a month, a season, or a year (in or about June 2019). Pleaders keep the same hedge and swap the governing preposition to match the size of the object, exactly as ordinary English does with on Tuesday against in June. In ordinary prose write around or sometime in — sometime in June 2019 is what a newspaper prints.
entries.see also: on or about, around, about, circa, in

entries.meaning: The deadline phrase of American legal and administrative English. It names the last acceptable moment and includes it. Because it is explicit about inclusion, it is the safe form whenever the difference between two adjacent days has money or a right attached to it.
examples: Proposals must be received no later than 5 p.m. on March 3.
The tenant shall give notice no later than thirty days before the lease ends.
Please submit the reimbursement form no later than the end of the quarter.
Report to the gate no later than forty minutes before departure.
No later than Friday, we need a decision from the board.
Payment is due not later than the fifteenth of each month.
Bids may be filed no earlier than March 1 and no later than March 15.

senses.head: By a stated date or clock time, that date included
body: Proposals must be received no later than 5 p.m. on March 3.

senses.head: By a point measured off another event
body: The tenant shall give notice no later than thirty days before the lease ends.

Sense 2 is the drafting workhorse, and it is where learners slip: the measured phrase is still naming a point, not a length. No later than thirty days before closing picks a square on the calendar; no later than thirty days picks nothing and should be within thirty days.
examples: Proposals must be received no later than 5 p.m. on March 3.
The tenant shall give notice no later than thirty days before the lease ends.
Please submit the reimbursement form no later than the end of the quarter.
Report to the gate no later than forty minutes before departure.
No later than Friday, we need a decision from the board.
Payment is due not later than the fifteenth of each month.
Bids may be filed no earlier than March 1 and no later than March 15.

entries.pronunciation note: than always reduces to /ðən/ — never a full THAN
entries.русский: не позднее — крайний срок, названная дата или время включаются
entries.register: formal — contracts, procurement, military, official notices
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a point in time: a date, a clock time, or a named event (no later than close of business). No gerund, no finite clause. Not a length of time — no later than three hours is an error for within three hours.
entries.pattern: [obligation] no later than [point in time] · No later than [date], [clause] · NLT [date] (military and government shorthand)
entries.variants: not later than (the older form, standard in statutes and regulations), NLT (abbreviation, US military and federal usage), no earlier than (the mirror form, which opens a window instead of closing one; a pair of them fixes both edges)
entries.contrast: It is by with the ambiguity drafted out. By Friday leaves a reader wondering whether Friday itself counts; no later than Friday includes Friday and closes the question, which is exactly why contracts use the longer phrase. Against before, which excludes the stated day and is therefore a day tighter. Against within, which measures an interval from now rather than naming a fixed date.
entries.see also: by, until, through, within, up to, on or about

entries.meaning: On the stated date, or close enough to it that the difference does not matter legally. It is one of the few phrases in English whose entire purpose is to preserve a claim against an imprecise memory, and it is nearly invariable in American criminal charging documents.
examples: On or about June 3, the defendant deposited the check.
The parties entered into the agreement on or about January 15, 2019.
She was last seen on or about the evening of the fourteenth.
Delivery is scheduled to occur on or about the first of the month.
On or about that date, the account was closed and the funds withdrawn.
Closing shall occur on or about October 15, subject to the lender's schedule.
The complaint alleges that the calls began on or about the first week of April.

senses.head: On a stated past date, or near enough that the difference is immaterial — the pleading use
body: On or about June 3, the defendant deposited the check.

senses.head: On a scheduled future date, allowing for slippage — the contract use
body: Delivery is scheduled to occur on or about the first of the month.

Sense 1 protects an allegation from a witness's imperfect memory; sense 2 protects a promise from a carrier's imperfect logistics. Both are hedges, and neither belongs outside a legal document — in ordinary prose, write around.
examples: On or about June 3, the defendant deposited the check.
The parties entered into the agreement on or about January 15, 2019.
She was last seen on or about the evening of the fourteenth.
Delivery is scheduled to occur on or about the first of the month.
On or about that date, the account was closed and the funds withdrawn.
Closing shall occur on or about October 15, subject to the lender's schedule.
The complaint alleges that the calls began on or about the first week of April.

entries.pronunciation note: or reduces to /ər/
entries.русский: юр. такого-то числа или около того — когда точная дата несущественна
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a date, and essentially nothing else. No clock time in ordinary use, no gerund, no clause.
entries.pattern: on or about [date] · [clause] on or about [date] · On or about [date], [clause]
entries.contrast: It is about with a legal safety net. About June 3 hedges and leaves June 3 itself sounding excluded; on or about June 3 hedges while conceding that the exact day may have been June 3 after all. Pleaders use it so that a date proved to be off by a day does not defeat the allegation. In ordinary prose around June 3 says the same thing without sounding like a subpoena.
entries.see also: about, around, circa, no later than, on

entries.meaning: On the stated day, or any day later than it. American statutes and regulations use it to fix the first day a new rule bites; insurance and tax drafting use it to sort events into the old regime or the new one along a bright line.
examples: The amendment applies to tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2026.
The policy covers claims first made on or after the retroactive date.
Any purchase made on or after the closing is for the buyer's account.
Tickets bought on or after the price change are nonrefundable.
On or after the effective date of this act, no new licenses shall be issued.
Employees hired on or after July 1 are in the new plan.
Deliveries scheduled on or after the fifteenth were canceled.

senses.head: Starting on a stated day, that day included — the effective-date use

senses.head: Of an event, occurring on the stated day or later
body: The policy covers claims first made on or after the retroactive date.

The two senses differ only in what is being sorted — a rule in sense 1, an event in sense 2 — and in both the whole work is done by the two words on or. Strike them and the boundary day becomes arguable, which in a tax year or a claims-made policy is worth real money.

The policy covers claims first made on or after the retroactive date.
Any purchase made on or after the closing is for the buyer's account.

entries.pronunciation note: or reduces to /ər/ and the two content words share the stress — AHN-er-AF-ter

entries.register: formal and legal — statutes, regulations, contracts, insurance policies, and tax rules
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a date or a dated event (on or after January 1, on or after the effective date). No gerund, no finite clause. Not a length of time: on or after thirty days is an error for no earlier than thirty days after or thirty days or more after.

That is the entire reason the phrase exists, and it is the same instinct that produced no later than and up to and including. Against from and after, the deed-and-indenture doublet, which starts an obligation running rather than sorting events into a window.

entries.meaning: On the stated day or any day earlier — a deadline with the last day explicitly counted in.
examples: Federal returns must be filed on or before April 15.
Rent is due on or before the first of each month.
Sealed proposals will be accepted on or before 5 p.m. on March 3.
Plaintiff shall serve the exhibit list on or before the tenth day before trial.
The option must be exercised on or before the expiration date or it lapses.
Any defect must be cured on or before the closing.
On or before December 31, the trustee shall distribute the year's income.

senses.head: By a recurring date, in a payment schedule

senses.head: By a date fixed off another event, in court orders and procedural rules
body: The exhibit list is due on or before the tenth day before trial.

Sense 3 is where learners slip, and the slip is the same one no later than invites: the measured phrase is still naming a point on the calendar, not a length. On or before the tenth day before trial picks a square; on or before ten days picks nothing and should be within ten days.

entries.register: formal and legal — contracts, court orders, tax filings, and official notices
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a date or a dated event (on or before April 15, on or before the tenth day of each month, on or before the expiration date). No gerund, no finite clause. Not a length of time: on or before thirty days is an error for within thirty days.

entries.meaning: Puts a time on the far side of a line: the minute hand past a number, the clock past midnight, a thing past the end of its useful life. The line is always there in the meaning, which is what separates past from the flatly neutral after.
examples: It's twenty past four.
The meeting starts at half past nine.
It was past midnight when they finally got in.
The kids were up way past their bedtime.
The milk is a week past its expiration date.
He's past his prime as a starter, but he can still relieve.
By then she was past caring what anyone thought.

body: It's twenty past four.

senses.head: Later than a stated time, with the sense of a line crossed
body: It was past midnight when they got in.

senses.head: Beyond the limit of a period, a condition, or a capacity
body: He's past his prime.
Sense 3 is where the word turns evaluative: past the deadline is a failure, past caring is exhaustion, past its expiration date is a warning. That judgment lives in past and not in after.

entries.complement: a noun phrase — a clock hour, a time point, or a limit. A gerund appears only in a closed set of idioms (past caring, past praying for, past believing). No clause. Past is also an adverb (he drove past), an adjective (the past week), and a noun (the past); the preposition has an object.

British colloquial gone six ("just after six") has no American equivalent. Beware the homophone passed, which is the verb: we drove past the exit but we passed the exit. Against after: past midnight stresses that a boundary was crossed, after midnight just names a later time. The movement sense (drove past the house) lives in past.
entries.see also: after, behind, beyond, till, of, to, past (movement)

entries.meaning: While waiting for, and until, the stated event. The word was modeled on French pendant, "hanging," and that is exactly the image — the situation hangs in place until the awaited thing lands.

He was held without bail pending trial.
Pending further instructions, the crew stayed on board.
The sale is final, pending a satisfactory inspection.
The grant is approved, pending a final head count.
Publication was delayed pending legal review.

body: He was suspended pending the outcome of the review.

body: The sale is final, pending inspection.

entries.complement: a noun phrase, characteristically one naming a decision or a process (pending approval, pending the outcome, pending trial, pending further review). No gerund, no clause. The same word is separately an adjective, both attributive (a pending lawsuit) and predicative (the case is pending); the predicative use is standard American.

Until takes a time point or a clause; pending takes the event itself, which is why pending approval works and until approval sounds clipped. entries.meaning: Up to a point in time, and then no further — identical in meaning to until.

body: The bar is open till two.

senses.head: Regional American clock time: minutes before the hour
body: ten till six

entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a point in time, or — as a conjunction — a finite clause (till the rain stops). Never a length of time: till three hours is an error for for three hours. No gerund.
entries.pattern: till [point in time] · from [time] till [time] · not ... till [point in time] · up till [point in time]

For the meaning, see the by/until rule under until. In American clock time, till is also a regional word for minutes before the hour: a quarter till three.

entries.meaning: Marks the far end of a state or an activity that runs up to it and then stops.
examples: The store is open until nine on weeknights.
We stayed until the last song.
Until last year, the road was gravel.
The offer stands from now until the end of the month.
He didn't call until Tuesday.
Nothing was decided until well after midnight.
She didn't find out until the movers were already loading the truck.
Up until the recount, she thought she'd won.
Up until about 1990, every one of those storefronts was a hardware store.

senses.head: Continuing up to a point in time, and stopping there
body: The store is open until nine.

senses.head: In the not … until frame, the point at which something finally happens

entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a point in time, or — as a conjunction — a finite clause (until she calls). Never a length of time (until three hours is an error for for three hours) and never a gerund (until leaving is not English; write until he left).

entries.contrast: by vs. until is the most useful contrast in this file. By is a deadline for a single completed action: Finish the report by Friday. Until marks a state or an activity that continues up to that point and then stops: Stay until Friday. The verb decides — punctual verbs (finish, submit, arrive, pay) take by; durative ones (wait, stay, keep, sleep) take until. Wait by Friday and finish until Friday are both broken. entries.meaning: Runs a stretch out to a stated edge and stops there — either the edge of a span already traveled or the ceiling on one still to come. Which of the two you get depends on whether the object is a point or a quantity.

Everything was fine up to last Friday.
Up to the very end he insisted the numbers were fine.
Delivery takes up to ten business days.

The lease runs up to and including December 31.
Coverage continues up to and including the last day of the month.
Up to the day he retired, he opened the shop himself.

body: Up to now, the plan has worked.

senses.head: No more than — a stated maximum length
body: Delivery takes up to ten business days.

senses.head: In the drafting phrase up to and including, out to a stated endpoint with that endpoint counted in

Sense 2 is the one that ends up in advertising and warranties, and it is deliberately weak: up to 40% off promises nothing except a ceiling. Read it as an upper bound, never as an estimate. entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a time point (up to now, up to last Friday) or a quantity of time (up to six weeks). No clause. Note that up to + gerund belongs to a different idiom entirely (up to no good, what have you been up to), as does the "your decision" sense (it's up to you).
