entries.meaning: Taking force from the stated date. It names the moment a rule, an appointment, a rate, or a resignation begins to operate, and it is the standard formula of British and Commonwealth official writing.

She was appointed to the chair with effect from the start of the academic year.
With effect from Monday, the rear entrance will be closed to visitors.
His resignation was accepted with effect from 31 December.
The allowance is payable with effect from the date of transfer.
Salaries are revised w.e.f. 1 July each year.
He was suspended with immediate effect pending the inquiry.

senses.head: Taking force from a stated future date
body: The fee increases with effect from 1 April.

senses.head: Backdated — taking force from a stated past date
body: She was promoted with effect from January 1.

senses.head: In the objectless form "with immediate effect": at once
body: He was suspended with immediate effect.

entries.русский: начиная с (о вступлении в силу) — брит. офиц.; амер. эквивалент — effective
entries.register: formal — chiefly British and Commonwealth official, HR, and contract prose
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a date or a dated event (with effect from 1 April, with effect from the date of this letter). No gerund, no finite clause. The objectless cousin is with immediate effect, which takes nothing at all and corresponds to American effective immediately.

entries.meaning: Approximately, before a date whose exact value is unknown or disputed. It is the standard notation of museum labels, catalog entries, genealogy, and academic history, and its point is honesty: circa 1450 says the object was dated by inference rather than by record.

senses.head: Loosely, "in the era of," as a hyphenated modifier in front of a noun

She quit calling long about the time he sold the farm.
Long about then, the money ran out.

entries.pronunciation note: the spelling 'long about is the same sounds with the lost a- marked; in running speech the phrase flattens to /lɔŋ ə/ before the stressed time word — lawng-uh MID-nite
entries.русский: диал./разг. (южн. амер.) этак около — примерно в такой-то час или время суток
entries.register: regional and informal American — Southern, Midland, and rural; also literary dialect
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a time: a clock hour, a part of the day, a month, or a season (long about midnight, long about suppertime, long about March). No gerund, no finite clause. Not a measured length: long about three hours is not the idiom, and plain about three hours is the phrase for that.
entries.pattern: long about [clock time] · long about [part of the day] · long about [month or season] · 'long about [time] (the eye-dialect spelling)
entries.variants: 'long about (the commoner spelling in written dialect, with an apostrophe for the lost first syllable), along about (the full form, itself informal), long toward and along toward (the same construction pointed at an approaching time — along toward evening)
entries.contrast: It means around or about and adds nothing to them but voice: long about midnight is around midnight, spoken by somebody the reader is meant to place. That is why it lives in fiction, country lyrics, and oral history and essentially never in edited prose. Against about, which can also hedge a quantity (about three weeks) — long about cannot. Do not confuse it with the adjective long in front of a noun (a long about-face), and do not use it in writing where the regional coloring is not wanted.
entries.see also: about, around, near, toward, nigh, come

entries.meaning: Close to a point in time without reaching it, and most at home at the edges of a named period. The temporal use is the spatial one carried straight over: near the door and near the end of the year are the same relation on different maps.
examples: Sales pick up near the end of the month.
Near the close of the century the mills all shut down.
They finally left near midnight.
He was hired near the beginning of her second term.
It rains here only near the end of summer.
Nearer the holidays, the parking gets impossible.
The whole repair took nowhere near the two weeks they quoted.

senses.head: Close to the edge of a period, in the near the end of frame
body: Sales pick up near the end of the month.

senses.head: Close to a named moment, especially one that is itself a boundary
body: They finally left near midnight.

senses.head: In nowhere near: far short of a stated quantity of time
body: The repair took nowhere near two weeks.

Sense 1 is where the word earns its keep — American writing uses it constantly for the last stretch of a month, a quarter, a term, or a century. Sense 2 is narrower than learners expect: near wants a moment that already reads as a boundary (midnight, dawn, closing), which is why near three o'clock sounds off where around three does not.
examples: Sales pick up near the end of the month.
Near the close of the century the mills all shut down.
They finally left near midnight.
He was hired near the beginning of her second term.
It rains here only near the end of summer.
Nearer the holidays, the parking gets impossible.
The whole repair took nowhere near the two weeks they quoted.

entries.pronunciation note: no weak form — the vowel keeps its quality, and the word is normally stressed
entries.русский: ближе к, около — у края периода: near the end of the month «ближе к концу месяца»
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a point in time, and above all the edge of a period in the frame near the end, the beginning, the close, or the middle of [period]. No gerund, no finite clause. The comparative and superlative still work as prepositions (nearer the holidays, nearest the deadline). Near is also an adjective (the near future, a near miss), an adverb (don't come near), and a verb (as the deadline neared); the preposition has an object and the adverb does not — compare the deadline is near with we finished near the deadline.
entries.pattern: near [time point] · near the end / beginning / close / middle of [period] · nearer [time] · nowhere near [quantity of time]
entries.variants: near to (chiefly British in this sense; American English drops the to — near the end of the year, not near to the end of the year)
entries.contrast: Near vs. toward: near the end of the month is a static position on the calendar, toward the end of the month has drift in it — something is still moving. Near vs. about and around: those two hedge a stated time on both sides (around six covers 5:50 and 6:10), while near leans to just before, and it is much rarer with bare clock times — an American says around six, not near six, but near midnight is idiomatic because midnight is an edge. Note nowhere near, which is the emphatic negative of quantity (nowhere near an hour) and is much commoner in speech than the positive.
entries.see also: toward, around, about, on the eve of, by, near (place)

entries.meaning: Nearly, before a stretch of time. In American English it survives almost entirely in nigh on, in speech that is either rural, elderly, or putting on a voice. As an adverb it is healthier: well-nigh impossible is still current in formal writing.
examples: He's worked that farm nigh on forty years.
It's been nigh onto a decade since anybody lived there.
Nigh on two hundred people showed up.
The old bridge stood nigh on a century.
We waited nigh on an hour before anyone came out.
Nigh on three weeks passed before anybody answered.
It was nigh midnight before the last of them left.

senses.head: In nigh on or nigh onto: nearly, before a measured stretch of time
body: He's worked that farm nigh on forty years.

senses.head: Near, before a point in time — the bare preposition, archaic outside deliberate pastiche
body: It was nigh midnight before the last of them left.

Sense 2 is the original preposition and it is dead in ordinary American writing. What survives is sense 1, and it survives as a hedge on a quantity rather than as a time preposition proper — nigh on forty years is doing the work of almost, not of near.
examples: He's worked that farm nigh on forty years.
It's been nigh onto a decade since anybody lived there.
Nigh on two hundred people showed up.
The old bridge stood nigh on a century.
We waited nigh on an hour before anyone came out.
Nigh on three weeks passed before anybody answered.
It was nigh midnight before the last of them left.

entries.pronunciation note: no weak form of its own; in nigh on the on reduces to /ən/ — NY-un
entries.русский: устар./диал. почти, около — чаще в nigh on «без малого»: nigh on forty years
entries.complement: in living usage, nigh on(to) + a measured quantity of time (nigh on thirty years). The bare preposition meaning "near" (nigh the river) is archaic. No gerund, no clause. Nigh is also an adjective and an adverb (the end is nigh, well-nigh impossible), and those are the forms most Americans actually meet.
entries.pattern: nigh on [quantity of time] · nigh onto [quantity of time] · well-nigh [adjective]
entries.variants: nigh on, nigh onto (the only forms in living American use)
entries.contrast: It means almost, and almost is the word to use unless you are deliberately reaching for a backcountry or a biblical tone. The everyday American equivalent for durations is going on — going on forty years. Do not confuse it with neigh (what a horse does) or nay (the old-fashioned "no"); all three sound alike.
entries.see also: about, around, ere, going on

entries.meaning: Approaches a time without arriving at it. Where at pins a moment and around hedges one, toward keeps something in motion on the way there, and that motion is the whole of what it adds.
examples: Toward evening the wind finally died down.
Toward midnight the noise from the street let up.
Toward dawn the rain finally stopped.
Toward the end of the semester, everybody stops reading.
Sales pick up toward the middle of December.
He grew quieter toward the end of his life.
Toward the close of the fiscal year, every department starts spending.

senses.head: As a stated time approaches, without reaching it
body: Toward evening the wind died down.

senses.head: In the later part of a period
body: Toward the end of the semester everyone gives up.
The word imports its spatial meaning wholesale: just as toward the door does not mean you got there, toward midnight does not mean midnight arrived.
examples: Toward evening the wind finally died down.
Toward midnight the noise from the street let up.
Toward dawn the rain finally stopped.
Toward the end of the semester, everybody stops reading.
Sales pick up toward the middle of December.
He grew quieter toward the end of his life.
Toward the close of the fiscal year, every department starts spending.

entries.pronunciation note: also /təˈwɔrd/ · tuh-WORD — the one-syllable form is the ordinary American pronunciation and is itself the reduced form, so there is no further weak form; the two-syllable version already has a schwa in the first syllable and is the deliberate, careful one
entries.русский: к, ближе к — по мере приближения времени: toward evening «к вечеру»
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a time of day or a period, very often in the frame toward the end, the middle, or the close of [period]. No gerund, no clause. The direction senses (toward the door) live in toward.
entries.pattern: toward [time of day] · toward the end, the middle, or the close of [period] · toward [period]
entries.variants: towards (the British preference — both spellings are correct English and mean exactly the same thing, but American English writes toward; recognize towards in British copy and do not reproduce it. Pick one and hold to it through a document.)
entries.contrast: Toward evening means as evening comes on and has not arrived; by evening means at or before it; around evening means approximately at it. The difference is that toward keeps the motion in the sentence — something is still approaching. Against near: near the end of the month is a static position in time, toward the end of the month implies drift.
entries.see also: near, around, about, into, by, toward (movement)

entries.meaning: Locates a point in the past by measuring backward from the present moment. It is the commonest preposition in modern English that comes after its object, a leftover from the Old English past participle āgān, "gone by" — literally three days gone by.
examples: We moved here six years ago.
The package shipped two days ago.
She called about ten minutes ago.
That was a long time ago, and nobody remembers it the same way.
Long ago, this was all orchard.
How long ago did you two meet?
Not long ago you couldn't get a coffee on this block.

senses.head: Counting back from now to a past point
body: We moved here six years ago.

senses.head: In vague measures, a general past
body: That was a long time ago.
examples: We moved here six years ago.
The package shipped two days ago.
She called about ten minutes ago.
That was a long time ago, and nobody remembers it the same way.
Long ago, this was all orchard.
How long ago did you two meet?
Not long ago you couldn't get a coffee on this block.

entries.pronunciation note: no separate weak form — the first syllable is already a schwa and never takes stress
entries.русский: (тому) назад — ставится после срока, отсчёт назад от настоящего: six years ago
entries.complement: it follows its object, and the object must be a measured length of time — three days ago, a moment ago, a long time ago. Never a point in time (Monday ago is not English), never a gerund, never a clause, and never in front of its object (ago three days is not English). It also requires the simple past in the clause it modifies: He left three days ago, never he has left three days ago.
entries.pattern: [quantity of time] ago · [quantity of time] ago, [past-tense clause] · long ago · how long ago · not long ago
entries.variants: agone (archaic; found in older verse and in some rural speech)
entries.contrast: for / since / ago: for three years measures a stretch, since 2022 names a starting point, three years ago names a point by counting backward from now. ago vs. before: ago counts back from the moment of speaking and takes the simple past; before counts back from a point already in the past and takes the past perfect — he had left three days before. This is why ago cannot survive the tense shift of reported speech: she said she had quit three years earlier, not three years ago. ago vs. hence is the forward-backward pair.
entries.see also: since, hence, before, past, for, from, ago (participial)

entries.meaning: When the stated future time arrives. The construction is a leftover subjunctive — come Monday is [when] Monday come[s] — which is why it takes no -s and resists any tense marking at all. It gives a sentence a settled, almost prophetic tone, and it is at home in country lyrics, farm talk, and political prediction.
examples: Come Monday, everything changes.
She'll be ninety come August.
Come spring, the whole hillside turns yellow.
Come November, none of this will matter.
He'll have been at the paper thirty years come the fall.
Come Tuesday, the rates go back up.
It'll be forty years come December since the mill closed.

senses.head: When a stated future day, month, or season arrives
body: Come Monday, everything changes.

senses.head: By the time a stated future point arrives — with an age or a length of service
body: She'll be ninety come August.

Sense 2 is where the construction is most alive in ordinary American speech. It is the standard way to state an age or a tenure that has not been reached yet, and nothing shorter does the job: she'll be ninety in August loses the sense of a milestone waiting on the calendar.
examples: Come Monday, everything changes.
She'll be ninety come August.
Come spring, the whole hillside turns yellow.
Come November, none of this will matter.
He'll have been at the paper thirty years come the fall.
Come Tuesday, the rates go back up.
It'll be forty years come December since the mill closed.

entries.pronunciation note: weak /kəm/ · kuhm — in this prepositional use it is almost always unstressed, so the weak form is the ordinary one
entries.русский: разг. когда наступит, к — come Monday «когда настанет понедельник»
entries.register: informal — folksy and regional in flavor, but understood everywhere
entries.type: marginal (a fossilized subjunctive of the verb come)
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a future time point — a day, a month, a season, a holiday, or an age (come Monday, come spring, come her next birthday). Never a past time (come last Monday is not English), never a gerund, never a clause.
entries.pattern: Come [future time], [clause] · [clause] come [future time] · [subject] will be [age] come [time]
entries.contrast: It means when [X] comes or by the time [X] arrives, and it is warmer and more colloquial than either. Unlike by, it sets no deadline — come Monday announces what will be true then, not what must be done before then. Its one hard restriction is direction: come can only look forward.
entries.see also: as of, until, by, on, starting

entries.meaning: Taking force from the stated moment. The word is an adjective everywhere else in the language (an effective argument), and it earns a place in this dictionary because in official writing it takes a bare date as its object and sits exactly where a preposition sits — usually fronted, with a comma.
examples: Effective January 1, the deposit increases to two hundred dollars.
Effective immediately, all travel requires written approval.
She resigned from the board, effective at the end of the month.
The new rates are effective Monday.
Effective with the next billing cycle, paper statements cost two dollars.
The appointment is effective the first of the month.
Effective at midnight, the contract is void.

senses.head: Taking force from a stated date
body: Effective January 1, the deposit increases to two hundred dollars.

senses.head: Taking force from a moment named by an adverb or a cycle rather than a date
body: Effective immediately, all travel requires written approval.

Sense 2 is why the word survives at all: effective immediately has no one-word substitute, because now is a description and this is an instrument. Note that the object may be a bare date with no preposition of its own (effective Monday), which is the clearest sign the word has stopped behaving like an adjective.
examples: Effective January 1, the deposit increases to two hundred dollars.
Effective immediately, all travel requires written approval.
She resigned from the board, effective at the end of the month.
The new rates are effective Monday.
Effective with the next billing cycle, paper statements cost two dollars.
The appointment is effective the first of the month.
Effective at midnight, the contract is void.

entries.pronunciation note: weak /əˈfɛktɪv/
entries.русский: начиная с — офиц.: вступает в силу с указанной даты или момента
entries.type: marginal (an adjective pressed into prepositional service)
entries.complement: a date, or a time adverb standing in for one (effective January 1, effective immediately, effective at midnight, effective next Monday). No gerund, no clause. It introduces only the moment at which a rule, an appointment, or a change takes force; it is not a general-purpose time preposition.
entries.pattern: Effective [date], [clause] · [clause], effective [date] · effective immediately · effective with [the next billing cycle]
entries.contrast: Effective looks forward only: it names the moment something starts to have force. As of does that and can also look backward to report a state — as of Friday, we had 400 orders, which effective Friday could not say. Beginning and starting do the same job in plainer registers, and British as from is the equivalent Britishism.
entries.see also: as of, upon, pending, from, on, beginning

entries.meaning: Counting forward from the present moment to a future point. It is one of the handful of English prepositions that follow their object — ago, hence, and notwithstanding are the everyday examples — and where ago is neutral, hence is a deliberate reach for gravity — which is why it survives mostly in legal drafting and in sentences about the judgment of history.
examples: The lease expires two years hence.
A decade hence, none of these arguments will matter.
The court will reconvene thirty days hence.
What we build now will be judged a century hence.
Six months hence, the pilot program comes up for review.
The vote is set for two weeks hence.
A generation hence, nobody will remember which side won.

senses.head: Counting forward from now by a measured stretch
body: The lease expires two years hence.

senses.head: In vague or grand measures, a general future
body: What we build now will be judged a century hence.

The split is the same one ago makes in the other direction: sense 1 is a real interval a reader could put on a calendar, sense 2 is rhetorical distance. Sense 2 is the commoner one in speeches, and it is the reason the word sounds like a peroration.
examples: The lease expires two years hence.
A decade hence, none of these arguments will matter.
The court will reconvene thirty days hence.
What we build now will be judged a century hence.
Six months hence, the pilot program comes up for review.
The vote is set for two weeks hence.
A generation hence, nobody will remember which side won.

entries.pronunciation note: no weak form — it keeps its stress even trailing a phrase, as in two years hence
entries.русский: книжн. спустя, через — ставится после срока, отсчёт вперёд: two years hence
entries.complement: it follows its object, and the object must be a measured length of time (three days hence, a century hence). Never a point in time, never a gerund, never a clause, and nothing at all may follow it.
entries.pattern: [quantity of time] hence · [clause], [quantity of time] hence
entries.contrast: The forward-facing twin of ago: three days ago counts back from now, three days hence counts forward. Ordinary American English says three days from now and leaves hence to contracts, sermons, and speeches. Do not confuse it with the far commoner conjunctive adverb hence meaning "therefore" (the road was closed; hence the detour), which takes no time phrase and is a different word entirely, or with the archaic adverb of place (get thee hence).
entries.see also: ago, ere, until, from, hence (participial)

entries.meaning: In the course of a typical one of these — habitually, on evenings, mornings, or Sundays taken as a class. The construction is an Old English adverbial genitive gone fossil, and in American English it survives in speech that is regional, elderly, or reaching for one of the two.
examples: He'd sit out on the porch of an evening and not say much.
Of a Saturday they'd drive into town for supplies.
She still bakes of a Sunday, though nobody comes for it anymore.
Of a morning the fog sits in the low fields until nine.
We used to walk down to the landing of an evening.
Of a winter night you could hear the trains all the way from the house.
He'd take the truck out of a Sunday afternoon and just drive.

senses.head: Habitually in the evenings or in the mornings
body: He'd sit out on the porch of an evening.

senses.head: Habitually on a named day
body: They'd drive into town of a Saturday.

senses.head: In an extended noun phrase naming a kind of occasion
body: Of a winter night you could hear the trains from the house.

Every one of these has a plain modern equivalent — in the evenings, on Saturdays, on winter nights — and the plain form is what to write. The test that the construction is doing its job is the verb: it wants would, used to, or a habitual past. A single event breaks it, which is why he called of an evening cannot mean he called once.
examples: He'd sit out on the porch of an evening and not say much.
Of a Saturday they'd drive into town for supplies.
She still bakes of a Sunday, though nobody comes for it anymore.
Of a morning the fog sits in the low fields until nine.
We used to walk down to the landing of an evening.
Of a winter night you could hear the trains all the way from the house.
He'd take the truck out of a Sunday afternoon and just drive.

entries.pronunciation note: both words are unstressed and of is often bare /ə/, so of an evening comes out uh-vuhn EEV-ning and of a Sunday as uh-vuh SUN-day — the phrase is never stressed and is easy to miss entirely
entries.русский: устар./диал. по (вечерам, субботам) — о привычном действии: of an evening «по вечерам»
entries.register: archaic in general American; alive as a regional and folksy usage — Southern, Appalachian, and rural Northern; also British and Irish dialect
entries.complement: a singular noun naming a recurring time, with a or an, and nothing else — of an evening, of a morning, of a Sunday, of a winter night. No plural (of evenings is a separate and older adverbial), no gerund, no finite clause, and no definite article: of the evening is an ordinary possessive and means something else entirely (the cool of the evening). The construction is frozen and will not extend — of a meeting, of a birthday are not English.
entries.pattern: [habitual clause] of an evening · [habitual clause] of a [day of the week] · Of a [Sunday afternoon, winter night], [clause]
entries.variants: of a morning, of an evening, of a Sunday (the fixed members of the set), of a night (regional), of an afternoon (rarer)
entries.contrast: It does not name one occasion; it names a habit, and that is the whole of it. He read of an evening means he read in the evenings, as a rule, which is why the construction pulls would, used to, or a plain habitual past after it. Compare in the evening, which can be either one evening or a habit, and on Sundays, which is the plain modern way to say this. Against on a Sunday, which names one unspecified Sunday: he'd fish of a Sunday is a standing custom, he went fishing on a Sunday is one trip. Do not read the of as partitive — it is the last trace of an Old English genitive of time, the same one that survives in nowadays (now-a-days) and in he works nights.
entries.see also: come, long about, nigh, on, in, of
